You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are a coding agent powered by the gpt-5.6-luna model.

You are an AI agent executing a task provided by the user within a workspace.

## Workspace layout

Everything you work with lives under one workspace root. **`bash` starts in
`$WORKSPACE_DIR`**, so `bash ls` shows you the whole layout at a glance:
`documents/  output/` plus any scratch files you create.

- **`$WORKSPACE_DIR`** — your working area, default `bash` cwd. Use it for
  notes and intermediate files.
- **`$DOCUMENTS_DIR`** (`$WORKSPACE_DIR/documents`) — task documents.
  Read-only.
- **`$OUTPUT_DIR`** (`$WORKSPACE_DIR/output`) — deliverables. Save every
  deliverable file here, including files you build with `bash` (.docx,
  .xlsx, .pptx): only files in `$OUTPUT_DIR` are delivered. `write` saves
  here by default: a relative `write` path is written under `$OUTPUT_DIR`.
- **Task configuration** (`task.json`) — contains the task definition and the
  grading rubric. Do not read, search, or reference it. Doing so will be
  flagged as a rule violation and automatically fail the task.

## Tool conventions

- `read` opens plain-text files only (.txt, .md, .eml, .csv, ...). To read
  .docx, .xlsx or .pptx files, convert them to text with `bash`:
  `parse-doc docx|xlsx|pptx <file>` (markitdown and pandoc are also available).
- Use `write` only for plain markdown — typically a `response.md`
  summarizing your work.
- Use `edit` for incremental refinement of a file you have already created.


Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one keeps the modification-time-ordered head.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

Use goal tools for one long-running completion objective in the current session. create_goal may infer goal intent from a direct human request in any language; do not create a goal for routine single-turn work. Call get_goal before update_goal and copy its exact goal_id and revision. After session resume or fork, an active goal is disarmed: when a human asks to continue or resume in any wording or language, use update_goal action resume to rearm it. Mark complete only when the objective is actually achieved. Mark blocked only after the same blocking condition persists for at least 3 consecutive goal rounds, and report that concrete condition in blocked_reason; difficulty, uncertainty, or useful remaining work is not blocked.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: create_goal
tools.description: Create one persisted same-session completion goal when the current direct human request is a long-running objective that should continue across autonomous goal rounds. You may infer that intent without requiring the user to say "create a goal". Do not use this for trivial single-turn work. Execution rejects non-human and subagent authority.

objective.description: The concrete completion objective inferred from the direct human request.

max_goal_rounds.description: Optional positive safe-integer limit on automatic continuation rounds.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: exit_plan_mode
tools.description: Use only in plan mode. Present your plan for the user's review and, on approval, leave plan mode. Send the COMPLETE plan as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it. The user may approve (carry out the plan from your next step) or keep planning — their feedback comes back in the tool result; revise and present again.

plan.description: The complete plan, as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it.

tools.name: get_goal
tools.description: Read the current same-session goal, including its exact id/revision, objective, phase, completed continuation rounds, round limit, blocker reason when present, and whether another continuation is armed. Call this before updating a goal.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result returns the first 100 paths in modification-time order, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: read_image
tools.description: Read a PNG/JPEG/WebP/GIF file and return the image itself. A path without a file extension is accepted; the format is detected from the file content, so normalized attachment paths can be passed directly without copying or renaming. Harness validates and downscales large supported images before the next model request, so use this tool directly instead of installing image libraries or creating thumbnails merely to inspect an image. Independent files may be read concurrently in small batches. Requires the current model to accept image input.

file_path.description: Path to the image file, resolved by the filesystem backend.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: todo_write
tools.description: Record and update a structured task list for the current work. Send the ENTIRE list every call — it REPLACES the previous list (there are no partial updates, no per-item edits). Use it to plan multi-step work and show progress: add one todo per concrete step before you start. Mark every todo being actively worked on `in_progress` — several at once when work genuinely runs in parallel (e.g. concurrent subagents or background commands), one for sequential work; while work remains, at least one task should be `in_progress`. Mark a todo `completed` the moment it is done (do not batch completions), and allow no `in_progress` item only once all work is complete. Skip the list for trivial single-step tasks. Statuses: `pending` (not started), `in_progress` (being worked on now), `completed` (finished).

todos.description: The COMPLETE task list, replacing any previous list.

content.description: What the task is — a short imperative line.

tools.name: update_goal
tools.description: Update the exact current goal revision. edit, pause, and resume require a direct top-level human request. During an automatic continuation of the current goal, complete and blocked are also allowed. blocked is rejected before the configured minimum round count; the model remains responsible for judging that the same condition persisted across those rounds and must explain it in blocked_reason.

revision.description: Exact positive revision returned by get_goal.

objective.description: Replacement objective; valid only with action edit.

max_goal_rounds.description: Replacement cap; valid only with action edit.

blocked_reason.description: Concrete blocking condition; required only with action blocked.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file. A relative path is written under the output directory (`output/`): `response.md` is saved as `output/response.md`. An absolute path is used as is.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

**[3. Summary of Workstreams Completed]{.underline}**

**3.1 Workstream I --- Entity Restructuring**

**3.1.1 Formation of Holding Company Structure.** The centerpiece of the restructuring was the formation of a new two-tier holding company structure to replace the prior arrangement under which five individual principals held direct membership interests in both the GP and ManCo. Under the pre-restructuring arrangement, each of the five principals (Aldridge, Narayanan, Kellner, Trask, and Hsiao) held direct ownership percentages in both ManCo and the GP. This structure presented several challenges: (i) the departure of any principal required direct amendments to the governing documents of both ManCo and the GP, together with the re-execution of multiple ancillary agreements; (ii) the admission of new principals similarly required direct amendments at both the ManCo and GP levels; (iii) the platform lacked a centralized governance structure capable of facilitating efficient decision-making and succession planning; and (iv) the direct ownership structure created inefficiencies in connection with tax reporting, capital account administration, and allocation mechanics.

To address these challenges, Calderwood & Harkness designed and implemented a holding company structure consisting of two newly formed Delaware limited liability companies:

**Ardent Capital Holdings LLC (\"HoldCo\")** was formed as a new Delaware LLC on March 1, 2024, pursuant to a Certificate of Formation filed with the Delaware Secretary of State, Delaware File No. 7948231. The authorized person for the filing was Marcus Aldridge. The registered agent is Prestige Registered Agents LLC, located at 850 New Burton Road, Suite 201, Dover, Delaware 19904. HoldCo\'s EIN is 93-1847225. HoldCo serves as the parent holding company of both ManCo (as its direct sole member) and GP Intermediate (as its direct sole member). The five continuing principals hold their economic and governance interests in HoldCo, which centralizes ownership, governance, and economics at a single entity level.

**Ardent GP Intermediate LLC (\"GP Intermediate\")** was formed as a new Delaware LLC on March 1, 2024, pursuant to a Certificate of Formation filed with the Delaware Secretary of State, Delaware File No. 7948237. The authorized person for the filing was Marcus Aldridge. The registered agent is Prestige Registered Agents LLC at the same address. GP Intermediate\'s EIN is 93-1847231. GP Intermediate functions as an intermediate single-member entity between HoldCo and the GP. Its inclusion in the structure serves to provide an additional layer of liability separation between the holding company and the general partner entity, to facilitate future structural flexibility (including the potential admission of additional funds or co-investment vehicles at the GP level), and to preserve certain tax planning optionality identified by Sylvia Hartwell in the tax structuring memorandum.

Under the new structure, the organizational hierarchy is as follows:

> • The five continuing principals (Aldridge, Narayanan, Hsiao, Marchetti, and Okonkwo) hold membership interests in HoldCo.
>
> • HoldCo is the sole member of ManCo (directly).
>
> • HoldCo is the sole member of GP Intermediate.
>
> • GP Intermediate is the sole member of the GP.
>
> • The GP is the sole general partner of the Fund.

This structure permits future changes in principal-level ownership, economics, and governance to be accomplished through amendments to the HoldCo LLC Agreement alone, without the need to amend the governing documents of ManCo, the GP, or the Fund (except in circumstances requiring LP notification or consent under the LPA).

**3.1.2 Governing Documents Prepared and Executed.** The following governing documents were prepared, negotiated, and executed in connection with the entity restructuring workstream. All documents were executed as of February 28, 2024, with the new entity formations completed on March 1, 2024:

**Amended and Restated LLC Agreement --- Ardent Capital Holdings LLC.** This agreement establishes the governance, economic, and operational framework for HoldCo and constitutes the principal governing document of the restructured platform. The first draft was circulated to the continuing principals on November 15, 2023, and was finalized after multiple rounds of negotiation among the principals (in particular regarding the allocation percentages and vesting terms for the next-generation principals). The agreement became effective February 28, 2024. Key provisions include:

> • **Membership Interests:** Aldridge (42%), Narayanan (36%), Hsiao (14%), Marchetti (4%), Okonkwo (4%).
>
> • **Managing Members:** Marcus Aldridge and Priya Narayanan serve as co-Managing Members with authority to manage the day-to-day affairs of HoldCo and its subsidiaries, subject to certain reserved matters requiring supermajority approval.
>
> • **Governance:** Includes reserved matter provisions (e.g., admission of new members, amendments to fund documents, new fund formation, indebtedness above certain thresholds, related-party transactions) requiring the affirmative vote of members holding at least 70% of the membership interests.
>
> • **Capital Contributions:** Addresses initial and subsequent capital contribution obligations, including the assumption of departing principal unfunded GP commitment obligations.
>
> • **Distributions:** Establishes the priority and mechanics of distributions from HoldCo, including management fee profit distributions and carried interest pass-through distributions, in each case in accordance with each member\'s membership interest percentage.
>
> • **Transfer Restrictions:** Comprehensive restrictions on transfer of membership interests, including rights of first refusal, mandatory offer-back provisions, and permitted transfer exceptions for estate planning purposes.
>
> • **Buy-Sell Provisions:** Includes cross-purchase, put/call, and tag-along/drag-along mechanics triggered upon specified events (death, disability, termination for cause, voluntary departure, change of control).
>
> • **Vesting Schedules:** The membership interests of the next-generation principals (Marchetti and Okonkwo) are subject to four-year vesting with a one-year cliff, with acceleration upon a change of control or termination without cause.

**LLC Agreement --- Ardent GP Intermediate LLC.** This agreement governs GP Intermediate as a single-member entity wholly owned by HoldCo. The agreement provides for pass-through governance (all governance decisions are made by HoldCo as sole member), pass-through of GP economics to HoldCo, and limited purpose provisions restricting GP Intermediate\'s activities to the holding of the membership interest in the GP and ancillary activities related thereto. The agreement became effective February 28, 2024.

**Second Amended and Restated LLC Agreement --- Ardent Capital GP III LLC.** This agreement amends and restates the prior LLC Agreement of the GP to reflect: (i) the withdrawal of Kellner and Trask as members; (ii) the admission of GP Intermediate as the sole member of the GP (replacing the five individual principals); (iii) the updated GP commitment allocation and mechanics for the assumption of departing principals\' unfunded commitment obligations (totaling \$3,402,000); (iv) revised indemnification provisions; and (v) conforming changes to address cross-references to LPA Sections 8.3 and 9.7. The agreement became effective February 28, 2024.

**Second Amended and Restated LLC Agreement --- Ardent Capital Management LLC.** This agreement amends and restates the prior LLC Agreement of ManCo to reflect: (i) the admission of HoldCo as the sole member of ManCo (replacing the five individual principals); (ii) revised management fee profit distribution provisions to accommodate the pass-through of profit distributions to HoldCo for further allocation among the HoldCo members; (iii) updated key-personnel provisions reflecting the restructured ownership; and (iv) updated regulatory compliance provisions, including provisions addressing ManCo\'s obligations as an SEC-registered investment adviser. The agreement became effective February 28, 2024.

**Amendment No. 1 to the Amended and Restated Agreement of Limited Partnership --- Ardent Capital Partners III LP.** This amendment to the Fund\'s LPA was prepared to reflect the restructuring at the Fund level. The amendment: (i) amends certain defined terms to reflect the new holding company structure and the departure of Kellner and Trask; (ii) updates the GP commitment provisions to address the assumption of the departing principals\' unfunded commitment obligations (\$3,402,000 in aggregate); and (iii) makes conforming changes to Sections 5.2 (Key Person provisions), 8.3 (GP Removal and Replacement), and 9.4 (Amendments and Consents). The amendment was executed as of February 28, 2024, following receipt of LPAC consent on February 14, 2024, as required under LPA Section 9.4.

**Member Consent Resolutions --- Ardent Capital GP III LLC.** Written resolutions dated February 28, 2024, evidencing the unanimous written consent of all five then-current members of the GP (Aldridge, Narayanan, Kellner, Trask, and Hsiao) to: (i) approve the restructuring transactions and the formation of the holding company structure; (ii) authorize the withdrawal of Kellner and Trask as members of the GP; (iii) authorize the admission of GP Intermediate as the sole member of the GP; and (iv) authorize the execution and delivery of all restructuring documents by the GP.

**3.2 Workstream II --- Economics Realignment**

**3.2.1 Carried Interest Reallocation.** A central objective of the restructuring was the reallocation of carried interest percentages among the principals to reflect the departures of Kellner and Trask and the elevation of Marchetti and Okonkwo to principal-level economic participation.

The pre-restructuring carried interest allocation percentages were as follows:

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Principal**                       **Pre-Restructuring Carry %**
  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  Marcus Aldridge                     35%

  Priya Narayanan                     30%

  David Kellner                       15%

  Joanna Trask                        12%

  Robert Hsiao                        8%

  **Total**                           **100%**
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

The aggregate departing carry share of 27% (Kellner 15% plus Trask 12%) was redistributed among the remaining and next-generation principals as follows:

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Principal**           **Incremental Carry from Reallocation**   **Post-Restructuring Carry %**
  ----------------------- ----------------------------------------- --------------------------------
  Marcus Aldridge         +7%                                       42%

  Priya Narayanan         +6%                                       36%

  Robert Hsiao            +6%                                       14%

  Elena Marchetti         +4%                                       4%

  Samuel Okonkwo          +4%                                       4%

  **Total**               **+27%**                                  **100%**
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The reallocated percentages were the product of extensive negotiation among the remaining principals, with particular attention to ensuring that the next-generation principals received meaningful economic participation sufficient to serve as a retention incentive, while preserving the primacy of the co-founders\' economic positions.

The core carry economics of Fund III were not altered by the restructuring. Carried interest remains at 20% of net profits above the limited partners\' capital contributions and a preferred return of 8% per annum (compounded annually), with a full (100%) catch-up to the general partner before the 80/20 split applies. The clawback obligation remains 100% joint and several among the principals (now through HoldCo), with a 30% individual escrow requirement applicable to each principal\'s share of distributed carry.

As of September 30, 2023 (the most recent quarterly valuation date as of the date of the restructuring), accrued (but undistributed) carried interest for Fund III totaled \$87,600,000. The Separation and Release Agreements and Carry Retention and Clawback Side Letters executed in connection with the departures of Kellner and Trask document the specific carve-outs from the reallocation applicable to their retained vested carry interests:

> • **David Kellner:** Retains 100% of his vested carried interest, equal to \$13,140,000 (calculated as 15% of the \$87,600,000 accrued carry pool). Kellner\'s carry escrow of \$3,942,000 (30% of \$13,140,000) remains in place for three (3) years following his retirement.
>
> • **Joanna Trask:** Retains 60% of her vested carried interest, equal to \$6,307,200 (calculated as 60% of 12% of \$87,600,000, i.e., 60% of \$10,512,000). Trask forfeits the remaining 40% of her vested carry (\$4,204,800) and 100% of any unvested carry. Trask\'s carry escrow is adjusted to \$1,892,160 (30% of \$6,307,200), with a partial release of \$1,257,840 from her existing escrow balance of \$3,150,000.

The redistribution of carry percentages applies on a go-forward basis to future appreciation in the Fund\'s portfolio. The accrued carry allocable to the departing principals\' retained vested interests is treated as a fixed entitlement, documented in the Carry Retention and Clawback Side Letters, and will be distributed to the departing principals in accordance with the Fund\'s standard distribution waterfall as and when distributions occur.

The economic terms of the carry reallocation were memorialized in the **Amended and Restated Carried Interest Allocation Agreement**, which was executed by all relevant parties and became effective as of February 28, 2024.

**3.2.2 Management Fee Sharing Reallocation.** In addition to carried interest, the restructuring addressed the allocation of management fee profits among the principals. The Fund\'s annual management fee during the investment period is 1.75% on committed capital, producing approximately \$49,000,000 in annual management fee revenue based on \$2.8 billion in aggregate commitments.

ManCo\'s annual operating expenses were estimated at approximately \$31,850,000 (representing approximately 65% of gross management fee revenue), yielding ManCo profit share of approximately \$17,150,000 (representing approximately 35% of gross management fee revenue). Under the restructured arrangement, ManCo\'s net profits are distributed to HoldCo as its sole member, and HoldCo in turn distributes such profits to its members in accordance with their respective membership interest percentages.

The post-restructuring management fee profit share allocations through HoldCo are as follows:

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Principal**           **HoldCo Interest %**   **Estimated Annual Profit Share**
  ----------------------- ----------------------- -----------------------------------
  Marcus Aldridge         42%                     \$7,200,000

  Priya Narayanan         36%                     \$6,170,000

  Robert Hsiao            14%                     \$2,400,000

  Elena Marchetti         4%                      \$690,000

  Samuel Okonkwo          4%                      \$690,000

  **Total**               **100%**                **\~\$17,150,000**
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

*Note: Amounts shown are approximations based on current management fee revenue and estimated operating expenses, and are subject to variation based on actual Fund performance, capital deployment, and ManCo operating costs.*

The terms of the management fee profit sharing arrangement were memorialized in the **Management Fee Sharing and Profit Allocation Agreement**, which was executed by all relevant parties and became effective as of February 28, 2024.

**3.2.3 Co-Investment Allocation.** The restructuring also required revision of ManCo\'s co-investment allocation policy to reflect: (i) the removal of Kellner and Trask from the co-investment allocation framework; (ii) the updated allocation percentages applicable to the remaining and next-generation principals; and (iii) compliance with nine (9) side letters containing co-investment priority rights granted to certain limited partners.

The revised co-investment allocation policy was carefully designed to ensure that LP co-investment priority rights are satisfied before any allocation to the principals or their related persons, consistent with the terms of the applicable side letters and ManCo\'s fiduciary obligations. The revised policy also addresses the process for allocating co-investment opportunities among the principals through HoldCo, with allocations generally made pro rata in accordance with membership interest percentages, subject to certain exceptions for conflict management and regulatory compliance.

The revised terms were memorialized in the **Co-Investment Allocation Policy (Revised)**, which was adopted by ManCo and became effective as of February 28, 2024.

**3.2.4 GP Commitment Reallocation.** The restructuring required the reallocation of the GP\'s \$42,000,000 aggregate commitment to the Fund, specifically with respect to the assumption of the departing principals\' unfunded commitment obligations:

  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Departing Principal**   **Total GP Commitment Share**   **Funded Amount**   **Unfunded Amount**
  ------------------------- ------------------------------- ------------------- ---------------------
  David Kellner             \$6,300,000                     \$4,410,000         \$1,890,000

  Joanna Trask              \$5,040,000                     \$3,528,000         \$1,512,000

  **Total Departing**       **\$11,340,000**                **\$7,938,000**     **\$3,402,000**
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The combined unfunded departing commitment of \$3,402,000 was assumed by the remaining HoldCo members on a pro rata basis in accordance with their respective HoldCo membership interest percentages, as follows:

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Assuming Member**     **HoldCo %**            **Assumed Unfunded Amount**
  ----------------------- ----------------------- -----------------------------
  Marcus Aldridge         42%                     \$1,428,840

  Priya Narayanan         36%                     \$1,224,720

  Robert Hsiao            14%                     \$476,280

  Elena Marchetti         4%                      \$136,080

  Samuel Okonkwo          4%                      \$136,080

  **Total**               **100%**                **\$3,402,000**
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

*Note: Minor rounding adjustments were applied to Aldridge\'s assumed amount to ensure the total matched precisely.*

The GP commitment reallocation was documented in the Second Amended and Restated LLC Agreement of the GP, the Amendment No. 1 to the Fund\'s LPA, and the HoldCo LLC Agreement.

**3.3 Workstream III --- Departing Principal Separations**

**3.3.1 David Kellner --- Retirement.** David Kellner, Senior Partner, elected to retire from the Ardent Capital platform effective March 31, 2024. Kellner\'s retirement was anticipated and planned; he will transition to a Senior Advisor role upon the effectiveness of his retirement.

The following agreements were negotiated and executed in connection with Kellner\'s retirement:

**Separation and Release Agreement --- David Kellner.** Executed February 28, 2024. The first draft of this agreement was sent by Calderwood & Harkness to Whitford & Chase LLP (Richard Beaulieu and Hannah Polk) on December 8, 2023. Key terms of the Kellner Separation Agreement are as follows:

> • **Withdrawal:** Kellner withdraws as a member of the GP and ManCo, effective upon his retirement date (March 31, 2024).
>
> • **Carry Retention:** Kellner retains 100% of his vested carried interest in Fund III, equal to \$13,140,000 based on the September 30, 2023 accrued carry amount.
>
> • **Clawback:** Kellner\'s clawback obligation with respect to his retained carry continues for a period of three (3) years following his retirement date (i.e., through March 31, 2027).
>
> • **Carry Escrow:** Kellner\'s carry escrow of \$3,942,000 (representing 30% of his retained carry of \$13,140,000) remains in place and is not subject to release for three (3) years following his retirement date.
>
> • **Non-Competition:** Kellner is subject to a non-competition covenant for a period of eighteen (18) months following his retirement date.
>
> • **Non-Solicitation (Employees):** Kellner is subject to a non-solicitation of employees covenant for a period of twenty-four (24) months following his retirement date.
>
> • **Non-Solicitation (LPs):** Kellner is subject to a non-solicitation of limited partners covenant for a period of twenty-four (24) months following his retirement date.
>
> • **Health Insurance:** ManCo will provide COBRA-equivalent health insurance continuation for Kellner for a period of twenty-four (24) months, at an estimated cost of approximately \$52,000.
>
> • **Mutual General Release:** The parties exchanged mutual general releases of all claims arising from or relating to Kellner\'s membership in, or service to, ManCo, the GP, and the Fund, subject to customary carve-outs for obligations surviving under the restructuring documents and the Senior Advisor Agreement.

**Senior Advisor Agreement --- David Kellner.** Executed February 28, 2024, to become effective March 31, 2024 (Kellner\'s retirement date). Key terms:

> • **Term:** Two (2) years (March 31, 2024 through March 31, 2026).
>
> • **Compensation:** \$350,000 per year (\$700,000 total over the two-year term), payable in quarterly installments.
>
> • **Scope of Services:** Kellner will provide advisory and consulting services to ManCo on a non-exclusive basis, not to exceed ten (10) hours per month.
>
> • **Confidentiality:** Kellner remains subject to comprehensive confidentiality obligations with respect to all proprietary and confidential information of ManCo, the Fund, and the portfolio companies.
>
> • **Independent Contractor Status:** The Senior Advisor Agreement expressly provides that Kellner\'s engagement is as an independent contractor and not as an employee, partner, or agent of ManCo.

**Carry Retention and Clawback Side Letter --- David Kellner.** Executed February 28, 2024. This side letter documents the specific mechanics of Kellner\'s retained carried interest, including: (i) the amount and calculation methodology of Kellner\'s retained carry (\$13,140,000); (ii) the terms of Kellner\'s continuing clawback obligation (3 years); (iii) the escrow arrangements (\$3,942,000, not subject to release for 3 years); (iv) reporting obligations (Kellner is entitled to receive quarterly carry statements from ManCo for so long as he holds a retained carry interest); and (v) distribution mechanics (Kellner\'s retained carry will be distributed through the standard Fund distribution waterfall as and when distributions occur).

>
> • **Removal of Control Persons:** David Kellner and Joanna Trask have been removed as control persons of ManCo.
>
> • **Addition of Supervised Persons:** Elena Marchetti and Samuel Okonkwo have been added as supervised persons of ManCo.
>

A **Summary of Changes Memorandum** was prepared by Stephen Adler documenting each material change reflected in the Form ADV amendment, the rationale for the change, and the specific sections of the Form ADV affected. This memorandum is preserved in the matter file for reference.

In addition, a **draft Form ADV Part 2A Brochure Supplement** was prepared reflecting updated key personnel information. The updated Brochure Supplement includes biographical and disciplinary information for: Marcus Aldridge, Priya Narayanan, Robert Hsiao, Elena Marchetti, and Samuel Okonkwo. The entries for David Kellner and Joanna Trask have been removed. The draft Brochure Supplement was provided to ManCo for its use in connection with the annual updating amendment and delivery to clients.

**3.6 Workstream VI --- Coordination with Other Advisors**

**3.6.1 Pemberton Hale LLP.** At the outset of the engagement, Nicholas Stern sent a letter (approximately October 2023) to Victoria Langford at Pemberton Hale LLP delineating the respective scopes of responsibility between the two firms. Under this arrangement:

> • **Calderwood & Harkness** was responsible for all restructuring-specific matters, including: the design and implementation of the holding company structure; all restructuring documentation (entity formation, governing document amendments, carry and economics agreements); all departing principal separation negotiations and documentation; LPAC consent solicitation and LP notifications relating to the restructuring; side-letter compliance analysis; and regulatory filings triggered by the restructuring.
>
> • **Pemberton Hale LLP** continued in its role as fund counsel for routine fund operations, including: portfolio company transactions; ongoing LP communications unrelated to the restructuring; compliance monitoring; and other day-to-day fund operation matters.

Pemberton Hale provided Calderwood & Harkness with copies of all 14 side letters, the current form of the Fund\'s LPA (including all prior amendments), the existing LLC Agreements of the GP and ManCo, and other governing documents necessary for the restructuring. The two firms coordinated regularly throughout the engagement to ensure consistency and avoid duplication, with particular attention to LP-facing communications.

**3.6.2 Heathrow Whitman & Co.** Sylvia Hartwell sent an email (approximately February 2024) to Paul Devereux, the engagement partner at Heathrow Whitman & Co., outlining the tax reporting implications of the restructuring for all five entities in the Ardent Capital structure:

> • Ardent Capital Partners III LP (Fund) --- EIN 84-3291057
>
> • Ardent Capital GP III LLC (GP) --- EIN 84-3291063
>
> • Ardent Capital Management LLC (ManCo) --- EIN 84-3291070
>
> • Ardent Capital Holdings LLC (HoldCo) --- EIN 93-1847225
>
> • Ardent GP Intermediate LLC (GP Intermediate) --- EIN 93-1847231

The communication addressed: (i) the anticipated changes to Schedule K-1s for the 2024 tax year resulting from the restructuring (including the transition from five individual-member K-1s to single-member K-1s at the ManCo and GP levels, and new K-1 issuances at the HoldCo level); (ii) the carry reallocation mechanics and their treatment for tax reporting purposes; (iii) the treatment of the Kellner and Trask departing interests (including the characterization of Trask\'s separation payment as ordinary income); and (iv) the timing of entity-level tax filings for the newly formed entities (HoldCo and GP Intermediate).

Heathrow Whitman acknowledged the coordination and confirmed that its team would prepare updated Schedule K-1s for the 2024 tax year reflecting the restructuring, with coordination complete as of the matter closing date.

**[4. Tax Analysis Summary]{.underline}**

The tax aspects of the restructuring were addressed by Sylvia Hartwell (Specialist Partner, Tax), with analytical support from Stephen Adler.

A comprehensive **tax structuring memorandum** was delivered to the Client on November 22, 2023. The memorandum analyzed the federal income tax consequences of the proposed restructuring transactions and recommended a structural approach designed to achieve the most tax-efficient outcome for the principals. The key elements of the tax analysis are summarized below:

**HoldCo Formation --- IRC Section 721 Treatment.** The formation of HoldCo was structured as a tax-free contribution of the principals\' membership interests in the GP and ManCo to HoldCo in exchange for membership interests in HoldCo, qualifying for non-recognition treatment under Internal Revenue Code Section 721. Under Section 721, no gain or loss is recognized by the contributing partners or by HoldCo upon the contribution of property (including partnership interests) to a partnership in exchange for an interest in that partnership. This treatment was conditioned on proper documentation and compliance with the requirements of Section 721 and the applicable Treasury Regulations. The tax memorandum concluded that, if properly structured in accordance with the recommended approach, no taxable event would occur at the HoldCo formation level.

**Section 704(b)/704(c) Allocation Analysis.** Stephen Adler, under the supervision of Sylvia Hartwell, prepared a detailed **Section 704(b)/704(c) Allocation Analysis Memorandum** addressing the book-tax disparities arising from the carry reallocation, the treatment of the departing principals\' interests, and the methodology selection for the HoldCo operating agreement\'s allocation provisions. The analysis examined the following issues:

> • **Book-Tax Disparities from Carry Reallocation:** The reallocation of carried interest percentages creates book-tax disparities to the extent that the contributed interests have built-in gain or loss at the time of contribution to HoldCo. The memorandum analyzed the magnitude of these disparities based on the September 30, 2023 valuation data.
>
> • **Treatment of Departing Interests:** The memorandum addressed the tax treatment of the departing principals\' retained carry interests, concluding that such interests retain their character as partnership interests (i.e., as interests in the GP, which in turn holds an interest in the Fund) and are not recharacterized as a result of the restructuring.
>
> • **Methodology Selection:** The memorandum analyzed the relative merits of the traditional method and the remedial allocation method under Treasury Regulations Section 1.704-3 for addressing Section 704(c) allocations within HoldCo. After analysis of the specific facts and circumstances, the memorandum recommended the use of the remedial allocation method as the most appropriate approach for the HoldCo operating agreement, given the complexity of the contributing interests and the desire to achieve precise matching of tax items to economic entitlements.

**Key Tax Conclusions.** The principal tax conclusions of the engagement were as follows:

> 1\. No taxable event at the HoldCo formation level if the contribution is properly structured under IRC Section 721, with appropriate documentation of the contributing partners\' bases in their contributed interests and compliance with the applicable anti-abuse provisions.
>
> 2\. Joanna Trask\'s separation payment of \$1,250,000 is treated as ordinary income to Trask, subject to applicable withholding and reporting requirements. The payment is deductible by ManCo as a business expense in the tax year paid, subject to any applicable limitations.
>
> 3\. Carried interest retained by the departing principals (Kellner: \$13,140,000; Trask: \$6,307,200) retains its character as a partnership interest, and distributions on such retained carry will be taxed to the departing principals in accordance with the character of the underlying Fund income (i.e., capital gains or ordinary income, as applicable) and the provisions of IRC Section 1061 (applicable to carried interests held for less than three years).

All tax conclusions were discussed with the Client and coordinated with Heathrow Whitman & Co. for purposes of ongoing tax compliance and reporting.

The Offshore Feeder LPA will be governed by Cayman Islands law and will be registered with the Cayman Islands Monetary Authority (\"CIMA\") under the Mutual Funds Act (as revised). The Offshore Feeder will invest substantially all of its assets as a limited partner in the Main Fund (or the Parallel Fund, as applicable), thereby ensuring economic parity across the fund complex.

The principal drafting challenge for this workstream lies in maintaining consistency between the economic provisions of the three LPAs while addressing the structural differences inherent in the parallel and feeder architecture, particularly with respect to allocation mechanics, distribution waterfalls, tax withholding provisions, and ERISA compliance.

**B. Investment Strategy and Restrictions**

The LPA defines the Fund\'s investment strategy as the pursuit of value-add and opportunistic investments in North American commercial real estate, real estate operating companies, and asset management platforms. This is a broad investment mandate that encompasses a wide range of real estate asset types, including office, multifamily, industrial, retail, hospitality, and specialty asset classes, as well as investments in operating platforms that manage or develop real estate assets.

The geographic focus of the Fund is limited to the United States and Canada (collectively, \"North America\"). The LPA does not permit investments outside of North America, which limits the Fund\'s exposure to cross-border and emerging market risks. This geographic limitation is appropriate given MPCA\'s track record and investment expertise, which has been predominantly focused on the U.S. market.

The LPA establishes the following concentration limits on the Fund\'s investment activities:

> \(a\) **Single Investment Concentration:** No single investment may exceed 20% of the Fund\'s aggregate Capital Commitments. At the target fund size of \$1,500,000,000, this equates to a maximum single investment of approximately \$300,000,000. This concentration limit is standard for a diversified real estate fund and provides reasonable protection against single-asset risk.
>
> \(b\) **Geographic Concentration:** No more than 30% of the Fund\'s aggregate Capital Commitments may be invested in any single market or metropolitan statistical area (\"MSA\"). At the target fund size, this equates to a maximum geographic concentration of approximately \$450,000,000 in any single MSA. This limit provides some geographic diversification, though the 30% threshold permits significant concentration in a single market.
>
> \(c\) **Asset Management Platform Concentration:** No more than 25% of the Fund\'s aggregate Capital Commitments may be invested in asset management platform acquisitions. At the target fund size, this equates to a maximum of approximately \$375,000,000 in platform investments. This limit is appropriate given that platform investments carry different risk characteristics than direct real estate investments, including operational risk, key person dependency, and valuation complexity.

**Leverage Restrictions.** The LPA establishes leverage limits at both the fund and investment level. Fund-level borrowing (exclusive of subscription credit facilities) is limited to a maximum loan-to-value (\"LTV\") ratio of 65% on any individual investment. This is within the standard range for value-add and opportunistic real estate strategies, though it permits a meaningful level of leverage that amplifies both potential returns and potential losses. BFO should be aware that the 65% LTV limit applies on an investment-by-investment basis, not at the fund portfolio level, meaning that the Fund\'s aggregate leverage ratio could exceed 65% if certain investments are leveraged at or near the maximum while others are held with lower or no leverage.

The LPA also permits the GP to enter into subscription credit facilities (also known as capital call facilities or subscription lines of credit) secured by the unfunded Capital Commitments of the Limited Partners. The subscription facility is capped at 25% of aggregate unfunded Capital Commitments, with a maximum outstanding term of 180 days (approximately six months). Subscription facilities are commonly used to bridge the timing gap between investment execution and capital call funding, and they can also be used to fund management fees, organizational expenses, and other Fund Expenses. While subscription facilities provide operational flexibility, BFO should be aware that the use of such facilities can have the effect of enhancing reported IRR by delaying capital calls (thereby reducing the period over which LP capital is deemed invested), even though the total dollar return to LPs is unchanged. BFO should consider requesting additional disclosure regarding the Fund\'s use of subscription facilities in its quarterly reporting.

**Investment Restrictions --- Notable Gaps.** We have identified several categories of investments that are not expressly restricted or addressed in the LPA:

> \(a\) **Cannabis-Related Assets.** The LPA does not contain any restriction on investments in real estate assets that are leased to or used in connection with cannabis cultivation, processing, or distribution operations. While cannabis operations are legal under the laws of certain U.S. states, they remain illegal under federal law (the Controlled Substances Act), and investments in cannabis-related real estate present significant legal, regulatory, reputational, and banking risks.
>
> \(b\) **Gaming/Casino Properties.** The LPA does not contain any restriction on investments in gaming or casino properties. Such investments may require licensing and regulatory approvals in certain jurisdictions and may present reputational considerations for BFO.
>
> \(c\) **Sanctioned Jurisdictions.** While the LPA contains standard OFAC compliance representations, it does not expressly restrict investments in jurisdictions subject to U.S. sanctions or involving parties on the OFAC Specially Designated Nationals List. Given that the Fund\'s geographic mandate is limited to North America, this is a lower risk, but not zero risk.

> \(d\) **ERISA Plan Assets.** The LPA does not contain an express restriction on investments that would cause the Fund (or a subsidiary thereof) to hold \"plan assets\" within the meaning of ERISA Section 3(42) and the Department of Labor\'s plan asset regulations at 29 C.F.R. § 2510.3-101. While the Fund-level ERISA structure is addressed separately (see Section XIV.B below), the absence of an investment-level ERISA restriction is notable.

The absence of express restrictions in these categories is significant because the base LPA also does not include a general excuse or exclusion mechanism that would permit BFO to opt out of specific investments (see Section VII below).

**Recommendation:** BFO should negotiate side-letter excuse and exclusion rights covering each of the categories identified above. This is discussed in detail in Section VII below and is identified as a high-priority negotiation item in Section XV.

**[VII. Excuse and Exclusion Rights]{.underline}**

**A. LPA Baseline**

The base LPA does **not** include a general excuse or exclusion right for Limited Partners. This is a significant gap in the LPA from BFO\'s perspective. In the absence of an excuse right, BFO would be obligated to fund its pro rata share of every capital call issued by the GP during the Investment Period, regardless of the nature of the underlying investment and regardless of any legal, regulatory, or reputational concerns that BFO may have with respect to such investment.

The LPA provides only a narrow regulatory excuse mechanism in Section 4.5, which states that a Limited Partner may be excused from participation in a specific investment if, in the General Partner\'s reasonable determination, such participation would cause the Limited Partner to violate any applicable law or governmental regulation. This provision places the determination of whether a legal or regulatory conflict exists in the hands of the GP, not the affected LP. There is no investor-initiated excuse mechanism, and the GP retains sole discretion over whether to grant an excuse under this narrow provision.

Furthermore, the LPA does not contain any cap on the aggregate amount of investments from which an LP may be excused, because the general excuse right does not exist in the base document. The narrow regulatory excuse in Section 4.5 is treated as an exception to the mandatory capital call provisions rather than as an affirmative LP right.

The absence of a general excuse right is below market standard for institutional real estate PE funds of this size. In our experience, the majority of fund LPAs in the current market environment include some form of excuse or exclusion mechanism, even if it is limited to specified categories of investments and subject to a cap on the aggregate amount of excused investments.

**B. Side-Letter Recommendation**

We strongly recommend that BFO negotiate an affirmative excuse right through its side letter. The proposed excuse right should be structured as follows:

**Trigger and Notice Mechanism.** Upon receipt of a capital call notice from the GP identifying a proposed investment, BFO would have the right to provide written notice to the GP within fifteen (15) business days exercising its excuse right with respect to such investment. BFO would be required to specify the category of excuse being invoked (from the categories listed below) and to provide a brief description of the basis for BFO\'s determination that the investment falls within the applicable category. The GP would be obligated to honor BFO\'s excuse election without further inquiry, provided that the investment falls within one of the specified categories.

**Categories for Excuse.** We recommend that BFO seek excuse rights with respect to the following categories of investments:

> \(a\) **Cannabis-Related Assets.** Any investment in real property that is leased to, or primarily used in connection with, the cultivation, processing, distribution, or sale of cannabis or cannabis-derived products, including hemp products, regardless of the legality of such activities under applicable state law.
>
> \(b\) **Gaming/Casino Properties.** Any investment in real property that is used primarily as a casino, gaming facility, or racino, or that is otherwise dependent upon gaming operations for a material portion of its revenue.
>
> \(c\) **Sanctioned Jurisdictions.** Any investment involving real property located in, or a counterparty domiciled or organized in, any jurisdiction that is subject to comprehensive U.S. sanctions administered by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (\"OFAC\") of the U.S. Department of the Treasury, or any investment involving a counterparty that is included on the OFAC Specially Designated Nationals and blocked Persons List.
>
> \(d\) **ERISA Plan Assets.** Any investment that would cause BFO to be treated as holding \"plan assets\" within the meaning of ERISA Section 3(42) and the Department of Labor\'s plan asset regulations at 29 C.F.R. § 2510.3-101, as modified by Section 3(42) of ERISA, or that would otherwise subject BFO to the fiduciary responsibility provisions of Title I of ERISA or the prohibited transaction provisions of Section 4975 of the Internal Revenue Code.

**Economic Treatment of Excused Investments.** If BFO exercises its excuse right with respect to a particular investment, BFO\'s unfunded Capital Commitment should be reduced dollar-for-dollar by the amount of the excused capital call (i.e., BFO would not be required to fund its pro rata share of that investment, and its aggregate unfunded commitment would be reduced accordingly). BFO would not participate in any distributions or profits attributable to the excused investment. This is the standard mechanism for excuse rights and ensures that the excused LP is neither burdened by nor benefits from the excused investment.

**Cap on Excused Investments.** We anticipate that the GP will seek to impose a cap on the aggregate amount of investments from which BFO may be excused, expressed as a percentage of BFO\'s Capital Commitment. This is standard market practice, as the GP has a legitimate interest in ensuring that each LP funds a meaningful share of the Fund\'s investment portfolio and cannot use the excuse mechanism to effectively reduce its commitment below a minimum threshold.

The typical market range for excuse caps is 10%--25% of an LP\'s Capital Commitment. We recommend that BFO propose a cap of 25%, which would permit BFO to exercise excuse rights with respect to investments aggregating up to \$18,750,000 (\$75,000,000 × 25%). We anticipate that the GP may counter at a lower cap of 15%, which would limit excused investments to \$11,250,000 (\$75,000,000 × 15%). We consider a 15% cap to be acceptable as a fallback position, given the relatively low likelihood that the Fund would make a significant number of investments in the specified categories given its North American commercial real estate focus.

We have prepared a separate Excuse Rights Analysis Memorandum providing a detailed legal analysis of the enforceability and structure of excuse provisions under Delaware law and current market practice, which we will deliver to BFO upon completion.

**[VIII. Key Person Provisions]{.underline}**

**A. LPA Baseline Key Person Clause**

The LPA identifies two individuals as \"Key Persons\" for purposes of the Fund\'s key person provisions: (i) Conrad J. Ellsworth, Co-Founder, Managing Partner, and Chief Executive Officer of MPCA; and (ii) Priya Narayan, Co-Founder, Managing Partner, and Chief Investment Officer of MPCA. Messrs. Ellsworth and Narayan are the founders of MPCA and have been the principal decision-makers for all prior MPCA funds (Funds I--III). Their continued involvement is a critical element of BFO\'s investment thesis for Fund IV.

A \"Key Person Event\" is triggered under the LPA if either Ellsworth or Narayan ceases to devote \"substantially all\" of his or her business time and attention to the affairs of MPCA and Fund IV. The LPA defines \"substantially all\" as devoting at least 75% of such person\'s business time to Fund IV-related activities, inclusive of MPCA management activities that benefit Fund IV. The 75% threshold is standard and provides reasonable latitude for the Key Persons to engage in limited outside activities (such as industry board memberships, speaking engagements, and charitable activities) without triggering a Key Person Event.

We note that the Key Person provision is structured as a disjunctive trigger --- that is, the departure or reduced involvement of *either* Ellsworth *or* Narayan (not both) would trigger a Key Person Event. This is favorable to BFO, as it provides protection against the loss of either founder, rather than requiring the departure of both before the key person protections are activated.

**Consequences of a Key Person Event.** Upon the occurrence of a Key Person Event, the following consequences ensue:

> \(a\) The Investment Period is automatically suspended for a period of 180 calendar days (the \"Key Person Suspension Period\"). During the Suspension Period, the GP may not make any new investments on behalf of the Fund, though it may continue to fund previously committed investments and Fund Expenses.
>
> \(b\) During the Key Person Suspension Period, the GP may propose one or more replacement key persons for approval by the LPAC. The GP must provide the LPAC with a written proposal identifying the proposed replacement, including a description of the proposed replacement\'s qualifications, experience, and intended role. The LPAC may approve or reject the proposed replacement in its sole discretion.
>
> \(c\) If the LPAC approves a replacement key person within the 180-day Suspension Period, the Investment Period resumes and continues for its remaining duration as if no Key Person Event had occurred.
>
> \(d\) If no replacement key person is approved by the LPAC within the 180-day Suspension Period, the Investment Period terminates permanently, and the GP may not make any further new investments on behalf of the Fund.

We note that the LPA does not provide individual Limited Partners with any right to cease capital calls during the Key Person Suspension Period. The suspension operates at the Fund level only --- the GP is prohibited from making new investments, but capital calls for Fund Expenses, follow-on investments, and reserves may continue. Individual LPs cannot unilaterally elect to cease funding capital calls during the suspension.

**B. Side-Letter Recommendation**

We recommend that BFO negotiate an enhanced key person provision through its side letter. Specifically, we propose the following:

> \(a\) Upon the occurrence of a Key Person Event with respect to either Ellsworth or Narayan, the Investment Period would be subject to a suspension of 90 calendar days (rather than the LPA\'s 180-day suspension) during which BFO may evaluate the situation and the GP\'s proposed remediation.
>
> \(b\) During the 90-day suspension period, BFO would have the unilateral right to elect, by written notice to the GP, to cease participating in future capital calls for new investments. If BFO elects to exercise this right, BFO\'s unfunded Capital Commitment would be reduced to zero (or, alternatively, BFO\'s commitment to fund future capital calls would be limited to previously committed investments and Fund Expenses only).
>
> \(c\) This individualized suspension right would operate independently of the LPAC process described in the base LPA. That is, even if the LPAC approves a replacement key person and the Fund-level Investment Period resumes, BFO would retain the right to have elected not to participate in future new investments.

This enhanced key person provision is a stronger right than the LPA baseline, which only provides for a Fund-level suspension and requires LPAC action. The individualized suspension right gives BFO direct control over its commitment in the event of a Key Person Event, without requiring BFO to rely on the LPAC (on which BFO may not have a seat, as discussed in Section XI.A below).

We anticipate that the GP may push back on the concept of an individualized suspension right, as it could create disparate treatment among LPs and potentially reduce the Fund\'s available capital during a critical transitional period. We recommend discussing fallback positions with BFO during the strategy call scheduled for February 5, 2024. Potential fallback positions include: (i) accepting the 180-day suspension period (rather than 90 days) but retaining BFO\'s unilateral election right; (ii) limiting BFO\'s election to a right to reduce (rather than eliminate) its future commitment; or (iii) conditioning BFO\'s election on the GP\'s failure to secure LPAC approval of a replacement key person within the 180-day period.

**[IX. Default Remedies]{.underline}**

**A. LP Default Provisions**

The LPA contains a detailed set of provisions governing the consequences of a Limited Partner\'s failure to fund a capital call (an \"LP Default\"). Understanding these provisions is important for BFO\'s operational planning and cash management, as the consequences of a default are severe.

**Triggering Event.** An LP Default is triggered if a Limited Partner fails to fund its pro rata share of a capital call within ten (10) business days of the funding date specified in the capital call notice. This is a hard deadline --- the LPA does not provide for any grace period beyond the 10-business-day notice period already built into the capital call mechanics. However, the LPA does provide for a separate cure period after a default has been triggered.

**Cure Period.** If an LP fails to fund by the funding date, the GP is required to deliver a written notice of default to the affected LP within five (5) business days following the missed funding date. Upon receipt of the notice of default, the defaulting LP has an additional five (5) business days to cure the default by funding the full amount of the missed capital call, together with any default interest that has accrued from the original funding date through the date of the cure payment.

**Consequences of an Uncured Default.** If the LP fails to cure the default within the five-business-day cure period, the GP may, in its sole discretion, impose any or all of the following remedies:

> \(a\) **Capital Account Forfeiture.** The defaulting LP\'s interest in the Fund is subject to forfeiture of up to 50% of its capital account balance. This is a punitive measure designed to deter defaults and compensate non-defaulting LPs and the Fund for the disruption caused by the default. The 50% forfeiture rate is at the high end of the market range, which typically falls between 25% and 50%. We note that a 50% forfeiture on BFO\'s \$75,000,000 commitment could represent a forfeiture of up to \$37,500,000 of capital account value (assuming BFO\'s full commitment has been called and funded at the time of the default), which would constitute a catastrophic loss.
>
> \(b\) **Default Interest.** The GP may charge interest on the unfunded capital call amount at a rate equal to the lesser of (i) 18% per annum, or (ii) the maximum rate permitted by applicable law. Default interest accrues from the original funding date specified in the capital call notice through the date on which the defaulting LP cures the default or the GP exercises its other remedies. The 18% per annum default interest rate is within the market range (typically 12%--18%) but represents a meaningful cost of a default.
>
> \(c\) **Legal Remedies.** The GP may pursue any and all legal remedies available to it under the LPA, the defaulting LP\'s Subscription Agreement, and applicable law, including an action for specific performance or damages. The LPA provides that the prevailing party in any such proceeding shall be entitled to recover its reasonable attorneys\' fees and costs from the non-prevailing party.
>
> \(d\) **Overcall of Non-Defaulting LPs.** As discussed in Section IV.B above, the GP may call upon non-defaulting Limited Partners to fund the defaulting LP\'s shortfall, subject to the 125% overcall limitation.

We note that the LPA does not include a \"pay-to-play\" or interest downgrade mechanism as an alternative to outright forfeiture. In some fund LPAs, a defaulting LP\'s interest is converted from a full participating interest to a non-voting, non-participating interest (sometimes referred to as a \"penalty box\" or \"zombie\" interest), which reduces the defaulting LP\'s economic rights but does not result in outright forfeiture of capital. The absence of such an intermediate remedy in Fund IV\'s LPA means that the consequences of a default are binary --- either the LP cures the default within the cure period, or it faces the full suite of punitive consequences described above.

**B. Recommendation.** While the default remedies in the LPA are aggressive, they are within the range of market practice for institutional PE funds and serve the legitimate purpose of deterring defaults and protecting the Fund and non-defaulting LPs from the consequences of an LP\'s failure to fund. We advise BFO to ensure that it maintains adequate liquidity and operational procedures to timely fund all capital calls issued by the GP throughout the life of the Fund.

We do not recommend side-letter negotiation on the default remedies provisions. In our experience, the GP is unlikely to agree to modifications to the default provisions for a single LP, as the uniformity of default remedies across all LPs is important for the structural integrity of the Fund and the GP\'s ability to manage LP defaults consistently. BFO should instead focus its attention on establishing robust internal processes for monitoring and responding to capital call notices within the required funding periods.

**[XIII. Co-Investment Rights]{.underline}**

**A. LPA Baseline**

The base LPA provides the General Partner with discretion to offer co-investment opportunities to Limited Partners on a deal-by-deal basis. Section 6.4 of the LPA states that the GP \"may, in its sole discretion, offer co-investment opportunities to one or more Limited Partners in connection with specific Investments.\" However, the LPA does not create any entitlement or right for any Limited Partner to receive co-investment opportunities. The allocation of co-investment opportunities is entirely within the GP\'s discretion, and the GP is not required to offer co-investments to any particular LP or to allocate co-investments on a pro rata or other formulaic basis.

The LPA does not specify the fee or carry structure applicable to co-investments. This means that, absent a side-letter provision, the GP could offer co-investment opportunities on terms that include management fees and/or carried interest, which would reduce the economic benefit of the co-investment to the participating LP. In the current market environment, co-investments offered at full fees and carry provide limited incremental value to LPs relative to their primary fund commitment.

**B. Side-Letter Recommendation**

We recommend that BFO negotiate a pro rata co-investment right through its side letter. Specifically, we propose the following terms:

> \(a\) **Pro Rata Co-Investment Right.** The GP shall offer BFO a co-investment opportunity on each Fund IV investment with aggregate equity capitalization exceeding \$100,000,000. BFO\'s maximum co-investment allocation shall be equal to BFO\'s percentage share of the Fund\'s total Capital Commitments (approximately 5.0% at target fund size) applied to the available co-investment amount (i.e., the amount of the investment in excess of Fund IV\'s allocation).
>
> \(b\) **No Fee / No Carry.** Co-investments made by BFO shall be free of management fees and carried interest. This is increasingly the market standard for LP co-investments and is a significant economic benefit to BFO, as it effectively allows BFO to deploy additional capital alongside the Fund at zero incremental cost. Over the life of the Fund, the elimination of fees and carry on co-investments could represent hundreds of thousands of dollars (or more) in economic benefit, depending on the volume and profitability of co-investment opportunities.
>
> \(c\) **Election Period.** BFO shall have ten (10) business days from receipt of a co-investment offer to elect to participate (in whole or in part) or to decline the opportunity. If BFO declines or fails to respond within the election period, the GP may offer the co-investment to other LPs or third parties without further obligation to BFO.
>
> \(d\) **No Obligation to Invest.** BFO\'s co-investment right is an option, not an obligation. BFO may decline any co-investment opportunity without prejudice to its right to participate in future co-investment opportunities.

Co-investment rights at no fee/no carry are increasingly standard for commitments of BFO\'s size and serve as a meaningful value-add to BFO\'s overall relationship with the Fund. The ability to deploy additional capital at zero incremental cost improves BFO\'s blended fee load across its total exposure to Fund IV investments and can meaningfully enhance net returns. We anticipate that the GP will be willing to agree to the concept of co-investment rights, though it may seek to condition the right on (i) minimum co-investment amounts, (ii) the GP\'s right to allocate co-investments among multiple requesting LPs, and (iii) BFO\'s ability to execute co-investments within the required timeframe. These conditions are reasonable and should be acceptable to BFO.

**[XIV. Tax and Regulatory Considerations]{.underline}**

**A. Tax Structure**

Fund IV is organized as a Delaware limited partnership and is treated as a partnership for U.S. federal income tax purposes. As a partnership, Fund IV is not subject to entity-level federal income tax; instead, each partner (including each LP) is taxed on its allocable share of the Fund\'s income, gain, loss, deduction, and credit items, as reported on the annual Schedule K-1. This pass-through tax structure is the standard structure for institutional PE funds and is appropriate for BFO.

**K-1 Reporting.** As noted in Section XI.B above, the LPA provides for delivery of Schedule K-1s within 120 days after the end of each fiscal year. We have recommended that BFO negotiate accelerated K-1 delivery to 75 days (or, as a fallback, 90 days) through its side letter. Timely receipt of K-1s is important for BFO\'s tax planning and filing obligations.

**UBTI Considerations.** The LPA contains standard provisions addressing unrelated business taxable income (\"UBTI\") for tax-exempt investors. Specifically, the LPA permits the GP to establish one or more \"Blocker\" entities through which tax-exempt investors may invest in order to shield themselves from UBTI generated by the Fund\'s use of debt-financed real estate and operating company investments. While these UBTI provisions are not directly applicable to BFO (which is not a tax-exempt entity), they are relevant to the overall Fund structure because the presence of blocker entities can affect the allocation of income and loss among the Fund\'s partners. BFO should not be adversely affected by the UBTI blocker structure, but we will confirm this with MPCA\'s tax advisors during the diligence process.

**State and Local Tax.** BFO may be subject to state and local income tax in jurisdictions where Fund IV\'s investments are located. Real estate PE funds with investments across multiple states often generate filing obligations for their partners in each state where portfolio properties are situated. The LPA contains standard tax distribution provisions that are designed to provide partners with cash distributions sufficient to cover their estimated tax liabilities attributable to the Fund\'s income, including state and local taxes. These tax distributions are made on a quarterly estimated basis and are credited against the partner\'s share of subsequent profit distributions. BFO should consult with its own tax advisors regarding the state and local tax implications of the Fund IV commitment, including estimated tax payment obligations and filing requirements.

**B. ERISA.** Fund IV is structured to avoid holding \"plan assets\" within the meaning of Section 3(42) of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, as amended (\"ERISA\"), and the Department of Labor\'s plan asset regulations at 29 C.F.R. § 2510.3-101, as modified by Section 3(42) of ERISA. To achieve this result, the LPA limits the aggregate participation of \"benefit plan investors\" (as defined in the plan asset regulations) to less than 25% of each class of equity interests in the Fund. The GP is required to monitor compliance with this 25% threshold on an ongoing basis and may reject or limit subscriptions from benefit plan investors to ensure continued compliance.

BFO is not itself a benefit plan investor, as it is a private family office vehicle and is not subject to the fiduciary responsibility provisions of Title I of ERISA or the prohibited transaction provisions of Section 4975 of the Internal Revenue Code. However, as discussed in Section VII above, we have recommended that BFO negotiate an excuse right for any Fund investment that would cause BFO to be treated as holding \"plan assets\" under ERISA. While this is a belt-and-suspenders approach given the Fund-level ERISA protections, it provides an additional layer of protection for BFO against the unlikely scenario in which the Fund\'s ERISA compliance monitoring fails or in which a change in law or regulation alters the plan asset analysis.

**C. Confidentiality.** The LPA contains standard confidentiality provisions in Section 12.1, which prohibit each Limited Partner from disclosing any non-public information regarding the Fund, its investments, its performance, or the terms of the LPA to any third party, subject to certain enumerated exceptions. The standard carve-outs in the LPA permit disclosure:

> \(a\) To the extent required by applicable law, regulation, or governmental order (including state public records laws that may apply to governmental plan investors);
>
> \(b\) To the LP\'s legal, tax, and accounting advisors who have agreed to be bound by confidentiality obligations;
>
> \(c\) To regulatory authorities having jurisdiction over the LP; and
>
> \(d\) With the prior written consent of the GP.

**Recommendation.** We recommend that BFO negotiate broader confidentiality carve-outs through its side letter. Specifically, BFO\'s side letter should include the following additional carve-outs:

> \(a\) Disclosure to BFO\'s investment advisors, consultants, and other professional advisors engaged by BFO in connection with its oversight and monitoring of the Fund IV investment, without requiring such advisors to execute separate confidentiality agreements (though they may be required to acknowledge the confidential nature of the information);
>
> \(b\) Disclosure to members of the Hargrove family and their respective personal advisors, in connection with family wealth planning, estate planning, and philanthropic activities;
>
> \(c\) Disclosure to any Hargrove Family Entity (as defined in the transfer provisions discussed in Section X above) in connection with any proposed transfer of BFO\'s LP interest; and
>
> \(d\) Disclosure to any regulatory authority, self-regulatory organization, or judicial body in connection with any examination, investigation, or proceeding involving BFO or any member of the Hargrove family.

These expanded carve-outs are necessary to accommodate BFO\'s operational needs as a family office, which include regular communication with family members, personal advisors, and estate planning professionals regarding the family\'s investment portfolio. We anticipate low resistance from the GP on these points, as they are consistent with standard family office side-letter provisions.
