**[I. Purpose and Scope]{.underline}**

This memorandum has been prepared by Calderwood & Harkness LLP (\"C&H\" or the \"Firm\") for the internal files of Ironside Capital Management LP (\"Ironside\" or \"ICM\") to provide a comprehensive summary of the formation steps completed to date and the governance structure of ICM Cascadia Co-Invest, LP (the \"Vehicle\" or the \"Partnership\"), a Delaware limited partnership formed for the purpose of co-investing alongside Meridian Infrastructure Partners Fund IV, LP (\"Fund IV\") in the acquisition of 100% of the outstanding equity interests of Cascadia Renewables Holdings, Inc. (\"Cascadia\" or \"CRH\"), an Oregon corporation.

The Vehicle has been organized as a single-purpose, single-limited-partner co-investment vehicle designed to facilitate Ironside\'s participation in the Cascadia acquisition on terms that are more favorable to Ironside than those applicable to Fund IV\'s general limited partner base. Specifically, the Vehicle was formed to commit Three Hundred Million Dollars (\$300,000,000) to the acquisition, representing approximately 28.57% of the total equity commitment of One Billion Fifty Million Dollars (\$1,050,000,000). Fund IV is committing the remaining Seven Hundred Fifty Million Dollars (\$750,000,000), representing approximately 71.43% of the total equity commitment.

The acquisition target, Cascadia Renewables Holdings, Inc., is a Pacific Northwest renewable-energy and water-infrastructure platform with operations spanning the states of Oregon, Washington, and Idaho. The agreed-upon enterprise value of Cascadia is One Billion Nine Hundred Fifty Million Dollars (\$1,950,000,000), which implies an EV/EBITDA multiple of approximately 14.1x, based on Cascadia\'s fiscal year 2021 adjusted EBITDA of approximately One Hundred Thirty-Eight Million Dollars (\$138,000,000). The transaction is structured as a leveraged acquisition, with the equity component of \$1,050,000,000 supplemented by acquisition financing to be arranged separately.
This memorandum covers the following topics in detail:
> \(A\) formation steps completed and pending;
> \(B\) partnership structure and capitalization, including the economic terms negotiated for the Vehicle;
> \(C\) governance and decision-making authority of the General Partner and the Limited Partner;
> \(D\) fiduciary duties owed by the General Partner, including modifications to default duties under Delaware law;
> \(E\) voting rights of the Limited Partner;
> \(F\) mechanics for the removal of the General Partner, including removal for cause and the consequences thereof;
> \(G\) information rights of the Limited Partner under the LP Agreement and the Side Letter;
> \(H\) material impediment event, dormancy, and wind-down provisions; and
> \(I\) additional matters, including term and dissolution, distribution waterfall, transfer restrictions, and tax and regulatory considerations.

This memorandum is intended to serve as a comprehensive reference document for Ironside\'s internal records and should be read in conjunction with the separate memoranda prepared by C&H on tax structuring (dated July 20, 2022), ERISA analysis (dated July 27, 2022), and the placement agent agreement review (dated July 18, 2022).
**[II. Formation Steps Completed]{.underline}**
**[A. Certificate of Limited Partnership]{.underline}**

The Certificate of Limited Partnership of ICM Cascadia Co-Invest, LP was prepared by C&H and filed with the Delaware Secretary of State on July 22, 2022. The filing was accepted and processed on the same date, and the Partnership\'s legal existence commenced upon such filing in accordance with Section 17-201 of the Delaware Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act (\"DRULPA\"), 6 Del. C. §§ 17-101 *et seq.*
The key details of the filing are as follows:
> • **Name of Partnership:** ICM Cascadia Co-Invest, LP
> • **Delaware Secretary of State File Number:** 7439218
> • **Date of Filing:** July 22, 2022
> • **Employer Identification Number (EIN):** 88-3921457 (obtained from the Internal Revenue Service on July 23, 2022)
> • **General Partner Named in Certificate:** Meridian Infrastructure GP IV LLC, a Delaware limited liability company
> • **Registered Agent:** Cascade Systems, 160 Greentree Drive, Suite 101, Dover, Delaware 19904

The Certificate of Limited Partnership is in the standard form prescribed by DRULPA Section 17-201 and contains the name of the Partnership, the address of the registered office in Delaware, the name and address of the registered agent, and the name and address of the general partner. A certified copy of the Certificate of Limited Partnership has been obtained from the Delaware Secretary of State and is retained in the Firm\'s deal files.
**[B. Limited Partnership Agreement]{.underline}**

The Agreement of Limited Partnership of ICM Cascadia Co-Invest, LP (the \"LP Agreement\") has been negotiated between C&H (on behalf of Ironside) and Breckenridge Sloane & Pratt LLP (on behalf of Meridian Infrastructure GP IV LLC, the \"General Partner\" or \"GP\"). The LP Agreement is in final, execution-ready form as of the date of this memorandum and is scheduled for execution by all parties on July 29, 2022, coinciding with the first close of the Vehicle.

The LP Agreement is governed by the laws of the State of Delaware, specifically the Delaware Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act, 6 Del. C. §§ 17-101 *et seq.* The parties to the LP Agreement are:
> • **General Partner:** Meridian Infrastructure GP IV LLC, a Delaware limited liability company, serving as the sole general partner of the Partnership.
> • **Limited Partner:** Ironside Capital Management LP, a Delaware limited partnership, serving as the sole limited partner of the Partnership.

The LP Agreement comprises approximately sixty-two (62) pages, exclusive of exhibits and schedules, and addresses the full range of partnership governance matters, including capitalization, capital calls and contributions, distributions, management authority, fiduciary duties, indemnification, information rights, transfer restrictions, term and dissolution, and winding up. The material provisions of the LP Agreement are summarized in the sections that follow.
**[C. Ancillary Formation Documents]{.underline}**

In addition to the Certificate of Limited Partnership and the LP Agreement, the following ancillary formation and transaction documents have been prepared and are either executed or scheduled for execution:

**1. Side Letter.** A side letter agreement (the \"Side Letter\") between Ironside Capital Management LP, as the Limited Partner, and Meridian Infrastructure GP IV LLC, as the General Partner, has been negotiated and is in final form. The Side Letter is scheduled for execution concurrently with the LP Agreement on July 29, 2022. The Side Letter addresses the following key matters:
> \(a\) confirmation that no management fee is payable on the co-investment vehicle;
> \(b\) most-favored-nation (\"MFN\") provisions ensuring that Ironside receives terms no less favorable than those granted to any other co-investor in a parallel or successor vehicle;
> \(c\) enhanced reporting obligations, including quarterly status reports during any dormancy period and access to the GP\'s books and records;
> \(d\) wind-down election rights, including the LP\'s right to elect wind-down of the Partnership following an extended dormancy period; and
> \(e\) certain other protective provisions as described more fully in the relevant sections of this memorandum.

**[ARTICLE IX --- LIMITED PARTNER ADVISORY COMMITTEE (LPAC)]{.underline}**
**Section 9.1 --- Establishment and Composition**

The Partnership shall establish a Limited Partner Advisory Committee (the \"**LPAC**\") consisting of three (3) members. The members of the LPAC shall be appointed by the General Partner from among the Limited Partners or their designated representatives; provided, however, that Pellegrino Capital Group LLC shall be entitled to appoint one (1) member of the LPAC for so long as Pellegrino Capital Group LLC holds a Partnership Interest in the Partnership. LPAC members shall serve in a non-fiduciary, advisory capacity, except where specific approval or consent rights are expressly conferred upon the LPAC by this Agreement. For the avoidance of doubt, LPAC members shall not owe any fiduciary duties to the Partnership or to any other Partner by virtue of their service on the LPAC.
**Section 9.2 --- LPAC Functions**
The LPAC shall have the following functions and responsibilities:
\(b\) Review and approve (or disapprove) all other matters requiring LPAC consent as set forth in Section 7.3;
**Section 9.3 --- LPAC Meetings**

\(a\) The LPAC shall meet at least once per calendar year, or more frequently as the General Partner or any two (2) LPAC members may request. Meetings may be held in person at the offices of the General Partner, by video conference, or by telephonic conference, as determined by the General Partner in consultation with the LPAC members.

\(b\) The General Partner shall provide at least ten (10) Business Days\' prior written notice of each meeting to all LPAC members, together with a written agenda and copies of any relevant materials to be discussed at such meeting.

\(c\) A quorum for any meeting of the LPAC shall consist of a majority of the LPAC members (i.e., two (2) of three (3) members). Actions of the LPAC shall be taken by the affirmative vote or written consent of a majority of the LPAC members (i.e., two (2) of three (3) members).
\(d\) Actions may be taken by the LPAC without a meeting by written consent signed by a majority of the LPAC members, which consent shall be effective as of the date of the last signature.
\(e\) The General Partner shall prepare and distribute to all LPAC members written minutes of each meeting within fifteen (15) Business Days following such meeting.
**Section 9.4 --- Indemnification of LPAC Members**

Each member of the LPAC shall be indemnified by the Partnership on the same basis as Covered Persons under Section 7.9 with respect to any Losses incurred by such member arising out of or in connection with such member\'s service on the LPAC. LPAC members acting in good faith in the performance of their duties as LPAC members shall have no personal liability to the Partnership, the General Partner, or any Limited Partner for any actions taken or omitted to be taken in their advisory capacity as LPAC members.
\(a\) The General Partner may remove any LPAC member for Cause upon written notice to such LPAC member and the Limited Partner that appointed or designated such member.

\(b\) Any Limited Partner that appointed or designated an LPAC member may, at any time, designate a replacement for such LPAC member by written notice to the General Partner, and such replacement shall become effective upon receipt of such notice by the General Partner.

\(c\) In the event of a vacancy on the LPAC (whether by removal, resignation, or otherwise), the General Partner shall appoint a replacement LPAC member from among the Limited Partners or their designated representatives within thirty (30) days of such vacancy; provided, however, that any vacancy in the LPAC seat held by a designee of Pellegrino Capital Group LLC shall be filled by a designee of Pellegrino Capital Group LLC.

> \(iv\) During the ninety (90)-day period referred to in clause (iii) above, the General Partner shall consult with the LPAC regarding a management transition plan, including the identification and evaluation of potential replacement key persons and the impact of the Key Person Event on the Investment.

The \"**Term**\" of the Partnership shall commence on the date of the filing of the Certificate of Limited Partnership with the Secretary of State of the State of Delaware and shall continue until the tenth (10th) anniversary of the Closing Date (i.e., January 30, 2036), unless earlier dissolved pursuant to Section 11.2. The General Partner may extend the Term for up to two (2) additional one (1)-year periods (each, a \"**GP Extension**\"), subject to the prior written approval of a majority of the members of the LPAC pursuant to Section 7.3(e). If both GP Extensions are exercised, the maximum Term of the Partnership shall expire on January 30, 2038. The Term of the Partnership is intended to be co-terminous with the term of Fund IV as it relates to the Investment.

**(c) Partnership Representative.** The General Partner shall serve as the Partnership Representative under Section 6223 of the Code for all taxable years of the Partnership. The General Partner shall not settle, compromise, or take any position with respect to any tax audit, examination, or proceeding that would disproportionately adversely affect any Limited Partner without prior consultation with the LPAC. In the event the Partnership is subject to any tax audit adjustment, the General Partner shall, to the extent permitted by applicable law, elect to push out any imputed underpayment to the Partners under Section 6226 of the Code rather than paying the imputed underpayment at the Partnership level.

This Agreement may be amended, restated, supplemented, or otherwise modified only by a written instrument signed by the General Partner and by Limited Partners holding a majority-in-interest of the Aggregate Capital Commitments. No amendment that adversely and disproportionately affects the economic or governance rights of a particular Limited Partner (including such Limited Partner\'s Preferred Return, Carried Interest allocation, Capital Commitment, Partnership Percentage, or LPAC seat) shall be effective without the prior written consent of such affected Limited Partner. Notwithstanding the foregoing, the General Partner may amend Schedule A without the consent of the Limited Partners to reflect (i) the admission of additional or substitute Limited Partners, (ii) the withdrawal or removal of Limited Partners, (iii) permitted Transfers of Partnership Interests, and (iv) adjustments to Capital Commitments and Partnership Percentages resulting from any of the foregoing.

Except as expressly provided herein with respect to the indemnification of Covered Persons (including LPAC members) under Sections 7.9 and 9.4, nothing in this Agreement, express or implied, is intended to or shall confer upon any Person other than the parties hereto and their permitted successors and assigns any legal or equitable right, benefit, claim, or remedy of any nature whatsoever under or by reason of this Agreement.

The General Partner may enter into Side Letters with one or more Limited Partners. The terms of any Side Letter shall supplement and, where expressly stated therein, modify or supersede the terms of this Agreement solely as to the Limited Partner that is a party to such Side Letter. Side Letters shall not be deemed to amend this Agreement as to any other Limited Partner unless such other Limited Partner is expressly entitled to the benefits thereof pursuant to a most-favored-nation provision contained in such other Limited Partner\'s Side Letter or this Agreement. The General Partner shall notify the LPAC of the existence of any Side Letters (without being required to disclose the specific terms thereof, unless such disclosure is required by the terms of a Side Letter or a most-favored-nation provision). The General Partner shall use commercially reasonable efforts to ensure that the terms of any Side Letter do not materially and adversely affect the rights of any Limited Partner that is not a party to such Side Letter.

matches.line: It is noted for the record that as of the date of this memorandum, Fund IV\'s first close had not yet occurred, and the fundraising process was ongoing. BFO will not be participating in the first close or any subsequent close.

**Draft Subscription Agreement:** Owen Fischer prepared C&H\'s markup of the Fund IV form Subscription Agreement on March 10, 2024. The markup included BFO-specific representations and warranties (including representations that BFO is a \"qualified purchaser\" within the meaning of Section 2(a)(51) of the Investment Company Act of 1940, and that BFO is not subject to ERISA or otherwise a \"benefit plan investor\"), the commitment amount of \$75,000,000, and cross-references to the side letter as a supplement to the LPA. The markup was prepared for BFO\'s review but was never finalized, executed, or submitted to the Fund.

The allocation of time across the engagement team reflects the nature of the work performed. Theresa Kim, as lead associate, was responsible for the majority of the substantive legal analysis, including the LPA and PPM review memoranda, the side-letter drafting and markup process, and the preparation of the various strategy and analysis memoranda. Owen Fischer performed substantial work on the MFN comparison matrix, subscription document markups, and supporting research. Pamela Cross\'s time was concentrated on strategic oversight, key client communications, and review of major deliverables and draft documents. Nicholas Stern\'s involvement was limited to initial engagement review, periodic billing oversight, and consultation on select issues.

For informational purposes, it is noted that Fund IV\'s anticipated first close date remains April 30, 2024, and the final close deadline is October 31, 2024. BFO will not be participating in any closing of Fund IV. No further monitoring of Fund IV\'s fundraising timeline or activities is required by C&H.

Line 2008907: (b) Absence of Duress, Fraud, and Undue Influence. The agreement must not have been executed under duress, fraud, or undue influence. (Fam. Code § 1615(c)(2).) The alleged agreement is dated May 30, 2008, just fifteen days before the parties' scheduled wedding on June 14, 2008. The temporal proximity of the alleged signing date to the wedding date raises significant concerns about duress and coercion. As the California Supreme Court recognized in In re Marriage of Bonds, the presentation of a premarital agreement close in time to the wedding date is a significant factor in evaluating voluntariness, because the prospective spouse may feel compelled to sign in order to avoid the humiliation and disruption of canceling a wedding. Id. at pp. 31–33. Even if the document were otherwise valid, the close proximity to the wedding, coupled with the complete absence of evidence that Ms. Fonseca had time to consult with counsel or to consider the agreement's terms, would support a finding that the agreement was not executed voluntarily.

We note that the term sheet with Atlas Fintech was signed on October 4, 2023 — four days before the Peralta validation testing was completed and five days before the report was issued. The timing raises the question of whether Lumos had any obligation to inform Atlas Fintech of the product setback before proceeding to execute the SAFE. Because the SAFE was never executed and no investment was made, this question is moot as a practical matter. However, it is worth noting that if the SAFE had been executed after October 9 (the date of the Peralta report) without disclosure of the validation failure, Lumos's exposure to misrepresentation claims from Atlas Fintech would have been significantly more acute than its exposure to Vantage Peak — because in that scenario, Lumos would have had actual knowledge of the shortfall at the time of the representation. The fact that the Atlas Fintech SAFE was not executed is a fortunate outcome for the Company.

Conclusion: For the reasons set forth below, I strongly recommend that Lumos promptly and affirmatively disclose the Prism Core v2.0 product setback to all current SAFE holders. Non-disclosure is not a viable option given the contractual information rights provisions, the clear materiality of the product setback, the acute risk of fraud and misrepresentation claims under Delaware law and federal and state securities laws, and the potential for personal liability of the Company's officers and directors. Additionally, disclosure must precede any further steps toward execution of the SAFE with Atlas Fintech Syndicate, L.P., the prospective co-investor that has signed a term sheet but has not yet executed its SAFE.

We note that the near-final draft of the Proposed MSA (MSA-PDS-MCB-2023), as circulated on October 6, 2023, contained a Change of Control clause at Section 14.6, which would have permitted either party to terminate the agreement within thirty (30) days following the occurrence of a Change of Control event affecting the other party. While the Proposed MSA was never executed and therefore no contractual termination right was triggered, the underlying business rationale for inclusion of that provision — namely, the recognition by both parties that a fundamental change in ownership or control of a counterparty may materially alter the commercial calculus and risk profile of the engagement — is directly applicable to the present circumstances. The Vaulton acquisition of Pinecrest constitutes precisely the type of event that the Change of Control provision was designed to address, and MCB's decision to terminate the negotiation process is consistent with the principles reflected in that provision.

A significant mitigating factor in the financial analysis is the complete absence of transition or wind-down costs. Because the Proposed MSA was never executed and no binding agreement of any kind was entered into between MCB and Pinecrest, there are no contractual termination fees, early exit penalties, or wind-down obligations. No MCB data was transferred to Pinecrest's systems. No systems migration activities were initiated. No Pinecrest personnel were onboarded to MCB's environment. MCB's IT operations have continued to operate entirely within the Corwyn environment throughout the negotiation period, and the termination of negotiations will have no impact on MCB's day-to-day IT operations.

Argument: Actual damages from delay were minimal because NFA had not yet secured end-customers for Phase 2 and Phase 3 route segments. Meridian may argue that NFA suffered minimal actual damages from Phase 2 and Phase 3 delays because NFA had not yet signed definitive service agreements with customers in those geographic areas, and therefore the delay in network completion did not result in direct revenue losses. The response to this argument is twofold. First, the difficulty of proving actual damages is precisely the circumstance that supports the enforceability of a liquidated damages clause; Meridian cannot simultaneously argue that actual damages were low and that the liquidated damages provision should be struck down because actual damages are easy to prove. Second, even if NFA had not yet executed customer agreements for specific Phase 2/3 segments, NFA was actively pursuing customer opportunities in those markets, and the delay in completing the network hampered NFA's ability to make binding commitments to potential customers, resulting in competitive harm and lost business opportunities that, by their nature, are difficult to quantify.

Dmitri Pavlovich Sobchak served as the Head of FX Trading at Meridian Prime. Mr. Sobchak was born on February 22, 1985, is a United States permanent resident and Ukrainian national, and resided at 301 West 57th Street, Apt. 18B, New York, New York 10019. He was formerly an FX desk analyst at Bridgemont Bank NA, where he had worked with Zelenko. Sobchak was directly responsible for the fabrication of trade confirmations purporting to document FX forward and option transactions that were never executed and for the execution of unauthorized wire transfers to divert funds from Meridian Prime's accounts. Summary judgment on the fraud and alter ego claims was entered against Sobchak on January 10, 2024.

Fabrication of Trade Confirmations. Dmitri Sobchak, in his capacity as Head of FX Trading, fabricated trade confirmations purporting to document FX forward and option transactions between Driftwood and Meridian Prime. Many of these trades were never executed on any exchange or with any counterparty. The fabricated confirmations reflected positions that, if genuine, would have shown consistent profitability, thereby justifying Meridian Prime's requests for additional margin deposits and creating the appearance of a successful and growing trading relationship.

In his capacity as Head of FX Trading, Sobchak was directly responsible for the preparation and transmission to Driftwood of fabricated trade confirmations purporting to document FX forward and option transactions that were never executed. He was also involved in executing unauthorized wire transfers of funds from Meridian Prime's accounts. Sobchak's role in the scheme was integral: he fabricated the transactional documentation that formed the foundation of the entire fraud, creating the appearance of a functioning trading operation where none existed.

Sobchak is individually liable as a direct participant in the fraud. As Head of FX Trading, he was directly responsible for fabricating the trade confirmations that purported to document FX forward and option transactions that were never executed. These fabricated confirmations were the documentary foundation of the entire fraud — without them, the fictitious trading activity reflected on the monthly account statements would have had no supporting documentation, and the fraud could not have been sustained.

(1) Material Misrepresentation. The Defendants made material misrepresentations of fact by fabricating trade confirmations that purported to document FX transactions that were never executed, by issuing monthly account statements reflecting fictitious positions and fabricated profits, and by representing that Meridian Prime was registered with the NFA as a swap dealer when it was not. Each of these misrepresentations was material because it related directly to the existence, value, and management of Driftwood's assets.

Sobchak fabricated the trade confirmations and, leveraging his familiarity with Bridgemont Bank NA's systems from his prior employment there, facilitated the execution of unauthorized transfers from Meridian Prime's accounts. (Compl. ¶¶ 53–54.) Sobchak's knowledge that the trades reflected in the confirmations had never been executed is self-evident.

Fabricated Trade Confirmations. Defendant Sobchak, acting at the direction of Defendant Zelenko, generated fabricated trade confirmations that purported to reflect the execution of FX forwards and options transactions in the name of Driftwood. These confirmations were formatted to resemble legitimate trade documentation and contained fictitious trade details, including notional amounts, execution prices, settlement dates, and counterparty information. In reality, the trades reflected in these confirmations were never placed, never executed, and never existed. The fabricated confirmations were transmitted to Driftwood's operations team, which processed them in the ordinary course of business. (Anand Aff. ¶¶ 30–32; Ex. C; Hu Aff. ¶¶ 17–18.)

Misrepresentation of Material Fact. Over the eighteen-month fraud period from January 2022 through July 2023, Defendants generated and transmitted to Driftwood fabricated trade confirmations and monthly account statements that purported to reflect the execution of FX transactions, the status of open positions, and the total value of Driftwood's account at Meridian Prime. These documents were material in the extreme: they were the primary means by which Driftwood monitored its trading activity and exposure, calculated its net asset value, and made ongoing investment decisions — including the decision to continue depositing margin and maintain its trading relationship with Meridian Prime. The fabricated statements showed purported trading profits of $14.8 million and culminated in a reported account balance of $52.1 million as of June 30, 2023. In truth, the trades reflected on the confirmations had never been executed, the profits were entirely fictitious, and the actual account balance was $3.2 million. (Anand Aff. ¶¶ 30–35; Exs. C, D; Hu Aff. ¶¶ 17–21.)

Defendant Sobchak, as Head of FX Trading, fabricated the trade confirmations that purported to show FX transactions that were never executed. He also directly participated in executing the unauthorized wire transfers through which funds were diverted from Meridian Prime's accounts. Like Carvallo, Sobchak's involvement was direct, hands-on, and central to the operation of the fraud. (Anand Aff. ¶¶ 23–24, 30–32; Exs. C, F.)

"For the purposes of subdivision (a), it shall be deemed that a premarital agreement was not executed voluntarily unless the court finds in writing or on the record all of the following:

To authenticate the photocopy as a true and accurate reproduction of a fully executed premarital agreement between Teodoro and Marguerite, the contestants would need to present evidence establishing: (1) that an original premarital agreement existed; (2) that the original was signed by both parties; (3) that the photocopy is a faithful reproduction of the original; and (4) that the original has not been altered or modified since its execution. The contestants have not met — and, on the current record, cannot meet — any of these requirements. The photocopy itself, on its face, shows that it was not signed by both parties, which directly contradicts the claim that it represents a fully executed agreement.

Family Code § 1611 unambiguously requires that a premarital agreement be "signed by both parties." The photocopy produced by the contestants bears only one signature — that of Teodoro R. Fonseca. The line designated for Marguerite's signature is blank. On the face of the document, therefore, the agreement was never executed by Marguerite, and it does not constitute a valid premarital agreement under the CUPAA.

She has no recollection of being presented with such an agreement, of discussing the terms of such an agreement, or of retaining counsel to review such an agreement. Her testimony, if credited, is not merely the absence of evidence — it is affirmative evidence that no agreement was executed. This is a critical distinction. The contestants are not simply unable to prove execution; they face affirmative, competent testimony that execution did not occur.

The alleged premarital agreement fails on the most fundamental of these requirements: it is unsigned by Marguerite. A premarital agreement that is not signed by both parties is not merely voidable — it is void. There is no California authority permitting the enforcement of a premarital agreement signed by only one of the two parties. Moreover, the contestants have produced no evidence of adequate financial disclosure, independent legal counsel for Marguerite, or compliance with the seven-day waiting period.

This deficiency is fatal. A document bearing only one party's signature is, by definition, not an agreement "signed by both parties" within the meaning of Section 1611. It is at most a unilateral proposal, a draft, or an incomplete document that was never executed. The statutory language is clear and admits of no ambiguity: both parties must sign. See In re Marriage of Bonds, supra, 24 Cal.4th at p. 22 (discussing the statutory requirements for valid premarital agreements); see also Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 134 (a writing must be signed by the party to be charged).

(b) Absence of Duress, Fraud, and Undue Influence. The agreement must not have been executed under duress, fraud, or undue influence. (Fam. Code § 1615(c)(2).) The alleged agreement is dated May 30, 2008, just fifteen days before the parties' scheduled wedding on June 14, 2008. The temporal proximity of the alleged signing date to the wedding date raises significant concerns about duress and coercion. As the California Supreme Court recognized in In re Marriage of Bonds, the presentation of a premarital agreement close in time to the wedding date is a significant factor in evaluating voluntariness, because the prospective spouse may feel compelled to sign in order to avoid the humiliation and disruption of canceling a wedding. Id. at pp. 31–33. Even if the document were otherwise valid, the close proximity to the wedding, coupled with the complete absence of evidence that Ms. Fonseca had time to consult with counsel or to consider the agreement's terms, would support a finding that the agreement was not executed voluntarily.

The premarital agreement claim fails at every level — the document is unauthenticated, incomplete, unsigned by Ms. Fonseca, and fails to satisfy any of the statutory requirements for a valid and enforceable premarital agreement under California Family Code Sections 1610 through 1617. The Contestants have not met their burden of proof, and no amount of supplemental evidence can cure the fundamental deficiency that Ms. Fonseca never signed the document. **Evaluating LPA Classifications**

I'm considering the distinctions between drafted and executed Limited Partnership Agreements (LPAs). The reference to "LPA dated Dec 20, 2023" in the memo raises a question about whether it was signed or simply dated. In private funds, LPAs can be dated prior to the first close but executed then. The closing memo indicates the first close hasn’t happened yet, even though the General Partner (GP) can sign the LPA beforehand. The LPA is usually a bilateral agreement, signed by the GP at that close.

**Examining LPA Documentation**

I'm looking at the review lines which refer to the LPA as "dated" instead of "draft." The actual LPA seems to be missing from the file, perhaps because it's not relevant to the C&H matter. They might want to include it based on its date. However, the user specifically says to skip funds with LPAs never signed, so I'm thinking the focus is on excluding matters with draft LPAs, rather than just missing a signature page. For 1026, although there's no explicit "never signed" statement, it refers to a dated A&R LPA, which suggests it's signed and operative. However, just because the first close hasn’t occurred doesn’t mean the LPA isn’t signed. I need to check the email timeline for 1026 to gather more context.

The resulting structure should be durable and extensible, capable of accommodating the formation and operation of future funds (Fund IV, Fund V, and beyond) without requiring a further reorganization of the platform's core governance architecture.

3. Scalability concerns. Option A does not create a platform structure capable of supporting future funds. When Ardent raises Fund IV, for example, a new GP entity (Ardent Capital GP IV LLC) would be required. Under Option A's flat structure, each principal would need to be admitted as a direct member of the new GP entity, with separate LLC agreements, separate membership interests, and separate economic allocations — replicating the current complexity across multiple fund vehicles. This approach becomes increasingly unwieldy as the number of funds and principals grows.

2. Scalability. HoldCo can serve as the parent entity for future fund general partners and management companies without any further restructuring. When Ardent forms Fund IV, for example, a new GP entity (Ardent Capital GP IV LLC) can be established as a subsidiary of HoldCo (through a new intermediate entity, if desired), with all principal-level economics continuing to be governed at the HoldCo level. This extensibility is a critical advantage for a platform with multiple fund cycles ahead of it.

The choice of allocation method is critical for three independent but interrelated reasons. First, the rolling LPs — who hold approximately $680 million in net asset value and who are the partners contributing the appreciated portfolio company interests into the CV — are the partners who economically benefited from the pre-contribution appreciation, and Section 704(c) is designed to ensure that the tax consequences of that appreciation follow them. Second, the new investors — principally Garrison Secondaries Fund IV LP, which is committing $380 million of new capital to the CV — must not bear the tax burden of pre-contribution built-in gain that accrued before they entered the partnership. Garrison's counsel at Whitfield & Calloway LLP has made this a threshold condition to closing the transaction. Third, approximately $250 million of capital is flowing through blocker entities — specifically, PCV Domestic blocker Inc. and PCV International Holdings Ltd. — whose corporate-level tax exposure is directly affected by the allocation methodology selected.

The $1.202 billion spread between the aggregate fair market value ($1.34 billion) and the aggregate adjusted tax basis ($138.0 million) of the contributed portfolio company interests constitutes "built-in gain" within the meaning of Section 704(c). This built-in gain must be allocated among the partners of the CV in a manner that prevents the shifting of pre-contribution gain to non-contributing partners — specifically, to Garrison Secondaries Fund IV LP and any other investors who are contributing cash (rather than appreciated property) to the CV. The mechanics by which this allocation is accomplished depend critically on which of the three permissible Section 704(c) methods is elected in the CV's limited partnership agreement.

Garrison Secondaries Fund IV LP has specifically raised this concern in the context of term sheet negotiations. Douglas Whitfield at Whitfield & Calloway LLP has communicated to our deal team that Garrison's participation in the transaction is conditioned upon the adoption of an allocation methodology that provides full protection from pre-contribution gain allocations. The traditional method plainly does not satisfy this condition. Outlook, given the current valuation levels and the concentration of the portfolio in three high-growth software companies — whose valuations are subject to the inherent volatility of the technology sector — the probability of a ceiling rule distortion event under the traditional method is not merely theoretical but is a realistic possibility over the expected hold period of the CV.

Applied to the full portfolio ($1.202 billion of aggregate built-in gain), the remedial method guarantees that regardless of the ultimate sale prices of the Luminos, ClearArc, and Vectral interests — whether they are sold at, above, or below their contribution-date FMV — Garrison Secondaries Fund IV LP and any other non-contributing investors will never be allocated tax gain or denied tax loss attributable to the pre-contribution appreciation. This guarantee holds in all market scenarios, including a severe downturn in which the portfolio companies' values decline significantly from current levels.

Second, the remedial method directly and fully addresses Garrison's negotiating position. Garrison Secondaries Fund IV LP, through its counsel Douglas Whitfield at Whitfield & Calloway LLP and its investment principal Mitchell Adler at Garrison Capital Advisors LLC, has made protection from pre-contribution gain allocations an express condition of its $380 million capital commitment. This memorandum provides detailed instructions for identifying, collecting, and reviewing documents responsive to Items 4(c) and 4(d) of the Hart-Scott-Rodino Notification and Report Form (the "HSR Form") in connection with the proposed acquisition by Harrowgate Private Equity Fund IV, L.P. ("HPE Fund IV") of 100% of the outstanding membership interests of Ridgemark Capital Advisors, LLC ("Ridgemark" or "RCA"). The purpose of this memorandum is to ensure that the Item 4 document collection process is conducted efficiently, thoroughly, and in compliance with the requirements of the HSR Act and its implementing regulations, so that the Acquiring Person's HSR Notification Form can be filed on or before the target filing date described below.

The transaction is governed by the Membership Interest Purchase Agreement dated June 4, 2024 (the "MIPA"), among HPE Fund IV, as the buyer, Ridgemark, Jonathan Kessler, Priya Narayanan, the other employee partners of Ridgemark identified therein, and Thornfield Growth Partners, LLC, as the majority equity holder of Ridgemark. The MIPA contemplates the acquisition of 100% of the outstanding membership interests of Ridgemark by HPE Fund IV in a negotiated transaction.

The HSR filing is being made by Harrowgate Capital Management LLC ("HCM") in its capacity as the Ultimate Parent Entity ("UPE") of the Acquiring Person. HCM, as the general partner of HPE Fund IV and the entity that controls HPE Fund IV's investment decisions, is the appropriate UPE for purposes of the HSR notification. All entities within the "person" of HCM — including HPE Fund IV and its controlled portfolio companies — fall within the scope of the HSR filing obligations as described in this memorandum.

For purposes of Item 4(c), the "filing person" means HCM, as the UPE, and all entities included within the "person" of HCM. Under the HSR regulations, the "person" of HCM encompasses HCM itself, HPE Fund IV (as an entity controlled by HCM), and HPE Fund IV's controlled portfolio companies, to the extent they are within the same "person" as defined under 16 C.F.R. § 801.1(a)(1). This is an important point: it means that documents prepared by or for officers or directors of entities controlled by HCM — including, for example, Franklin Broussard, the CEO of Dunmore Asset Management LLC ("Dunmore") — may be responsive to Item 4(c) if they analyze the Ridgemark acquisition with respect to the enumerated topics.

Dunmore overlap. We wish to draw particular attention to the competitive overlap between Dunmore and Ridgemark. Dunmore Asset Management LLC is an existing HPE Fund IV portfolio company, acquired in 2023, headquartered at 227 West Monroe Street, Suite 4100, Chicago, IL 60606, with Franklin Broussard serving as CEO. Dunmore is a SEC-registered investment adviser with total assets under management ("AUM") of approximately $3.9 billion, of which approximately $2.1 billion is managed in alternative credit separately managed accounts ("SMAs"). Dunmore operates under NAICS code 523920 (Portfolio Management). Ridgemark, for its part, manages approximately $1.4 billion in alternative credit SMAs, also under NAICS code 523920. Any documents discussing competitive overlaps between Dunmore and Ridgemark — including discussions of combined market share, overlapping client bases, competing product offerings, or the potential for post-acquisition integration or repositioning — are almost certainly responsive to Item 4(c) and must be collected with the highest priority. Given the horizontal nature of this overlap, we expect that FTC staff will focus significant attention on this area during any review of the filing.

Cairnstone Advisory Group LLC. Cairnstone Advisory Group LLC ("Cairnstone") is Ridgemark's financial advisor, with Laura Feng, Managing Director, serving as the lead contact. Cairnstone's offices are located at 200 Clarendon Street, Suite 1500, Boston, MA 02116. Although Cairnstone was retained by Ridgemark (rather than by HCM), any materials prepared by Cairnstone that were shared with or provided to HCM or HPE Fund IV during the due diligence process — such as the sell-side CIM, management presentations, or market overviews — are responsive to Item 4(d) to the extent they discuss markets, market shares, competition, or growth potential. These materials were "prepared by" a third-party advisor and were used by HCM "for the purpose of evaluating or analyzing" the proposed acquisition.

Other consultants or advisors. If HCM or HPE Fund IV retained any other consultants, market research firms, or advisory firms in connection with the evaluation of the Ridgemark acquisition, any deliverables from those engagements that address the enumerated topics would also be responsive to Item 4(d). We are not currently aware of any such engagements, but custodians should flag any such materials if they exist.

Attorney-client privilege. Documents prepared by Calderwood & Harkness LLP in its capacity as legal counsel to HCM and HPE Fund IV are generally protected by the attorney-client privilege and the work product doctrine, and are not required to be produced under Item 4(c) or 4(d). However, this protection is subject to certain limitations. Documents that were shared with non-privileged parties (for example, shared with Greycastle or with Ridgemark management outside the scope of a common-interest agreement) may have waived privilege protection. Additionally, documents that contain factual analyses or competitive assessments that are separable from legal advice may be subject to production, even if prepared by legal counsel. C&H will screen all collected documents for privilege issues as part of the attorney review process described in Section VI below.

Harrowgate Capital Management LLC is the general partner of HPE Fund IV and the Ultimate Parent Entity for HSR purposes. HCM is the primary entity from which Item 4(c) documents will be sourced, as it is the entity whose officers and directors are responsible for evaluating and approving the Ridgemark acquisition.

HPE Fund IV is the acquiring entity under the MIPA. HPE Fund IV reached its final close in December 2023 with total committed capital of $6.2 billion. The fund's stated investment strategy focuses on middle-market financial services and asset management platform acquisitions. Ridgemark is expected to be the fourth platform investment for HPE Fund IV.

To the extent that documents were prepared at the fund level (as distinct from HCM) discussing the Ridgemark transaction — for example, limited partner advisory committee ("LPAC") materials, fund-level investment reports, or internal fund memoranda — those documents are responsive if they address the enumerated topics. In practice, we expect that most responsive documents will originate from HCM rather than from HPE Fund IV itself, given that HCM personnel are responsible for deal sourcing, evaluation, and execution. However, custodians should not assume that fund-level documents are outside the scope of collection.

Dunmore Asset Management LLC is an existing HPE Fund IV portfolio company. It is a SEC-registered investment adviser headquartered at 227 West Monroe Street, Suite 4100, Chicago, IL 60606. Dunmore's CEO is Franklin Broussard. Dunmore manages total AUM of approximately $3.9 billion, of which approximately $2.1 billion is allocated to alternative credit separately managed accounts. Dunmore operates under NAICS code 523920 (Portfolio Management).

Greycastle Partners LLC is the financial advisor to HCM and HPE Fund IV for the Ridgemark transaction. Mitchell Avery, Managing Director, is the lead banker. Greycastle's offices are located at 300 Atlantic Street, Stamford, CT 06901.

All materials prepared by Greycastle in connection with the Ridgemark acquisition are potentially responsive under Item 4(d). This includes, without limitation, pitch books, confidential information memoranda, market overviews, competitive landscape analyses, comparable transaction analyses, comparable company analyses, and financial models that reference markets, competition, or growth potential. Greycastle is a third party and is not within the "person" of the filing person for Item 4(c) purposes; however, documents prepared by Greycastle for officers or directors of HCM may be responsive under both Item 4(c) (as documents prepared "for" officers or directors) and Item 4(d) (as documents prepared by an investment banker). We will coordinate with Greycastle to obtain copies of all deliverables provided to HCM and HPE Fund IV, as described in Section VII below.

Mr. Broussard is the chief executive of Dunmore and may have been consulted by HCM or HPE Fund IV regarding the competitive overlap between Dunmore and Ridgemark in the alternative credit SMA and sub-advisory markets. He may have prepared or received analyses of Dunmore's market position relative to Ridgemark, integration scenarios, or competitive assessments in connection with the proposed acquisition.

Important note: Greycastle is a third party and is not within the "person" of the filing person for Item 4(c) purposes. However, documents prepared by Greycastle for HCM or HPE Fund IV are responsive under Item 4(d), and documents prepared by Greycastle that were directed to officers or directors of HCM may also be responsive under Item 4(c). 8. Consultant Reports. {"file_path":"response.md","content":"# Funds & Asset Management matters involving a fund with an LP advisory committee

## Answer

**3 matters** qualify.

I counted a matter when (1) the substantive engagement was a Funds & Asset Management matter, (2) the relevant fund or co-investment vehicle had an LP-side advisory committee (including an Investor Advisory Committee serving that function), and (3) the file showed that the relevant LPA was executed/effective—not merely a draft or proposed form.

| Matter | Fund / vehicle | LP advisory body | Signed-LPA basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1001-00002** | **Ardent Capital Partners III LP** | Limited Partner Advisory Committee (LPAC), four members | The matter closing memorandum says all restructuring documents were executed as of February 28, 2024. The LPA Amendment was effective February 28, 2024, following LPAC consent on February 14, 2024. |
| **1024-00002** | **Driftwood Absolute Return Fund Ltd.** | Investor Advisory Committee (IAC)—the fund's LP advisory committee equivalent | The fund was governed by an Amended & Restated LPA dated March 15, 2017. The First Amendment is an execution version effective August 26, 2024, and records the IAC's review and the requisite LP consents. |
| **1027-00002** | **Ridgeline-Clarion Co-Invest, L.P.** | LPAC, established by LPA §9.1 | The LPA is expressly titled “Execution Version,” dated January 30, 2026. The closing opinion and funds-flow memorandum confirm a January 30, 2026 closing and Pellegrino's $25 million capital commitment. |

## Matter-by-matter support

### 1. Matter 1001-00002 — Ardent Capital Partners III LP

**Why it qualifies.** This was a fund-platform restructuring and economics-realignment engagement. The engagement letter expressly included preparation of materials for notice to and consent from the Fund's **Limited Partner Advisory Committee** under LPA §9.4. The LPAC notification package states that the LPAC consented unanimously on February 14, 2024. The matter closing memorandum states that all restructuring documents were duly executed as of February 28, 2024.

**Key evidence relied on:**

- `documents/matters/1001-00002/Engagement & Administration/engagement-letter.docx` — identifies the Ardent Capital Partners III LP fund restructuring and the LPAC consent workstream.
- `documents/matters/1001-00002/LP Consent & Notification/lpac-notification-and-consent-letter.docx` — requests LPAC review and consent under LPA §9.4.
- `documents/matters/1001-00002/LP Consent & Notification/lpac-form-of-written-consent.docx` — records the LPAC written consent dated February 14, 2024.
- `documents/matters/1001-00002/Amended Governing Documents/lpa-amendment-no-1.docx` — Amendment No. 1 to the Fund LPA, effective February 28, 2024, following the LPAC consent.
- `documents/matters/1001-00002/Engagement & Administration/matter-closing-memo.docx` — confirms completion and execution of the restructuring documents and closure of the matter.

### 2. Matter 1024-00002 — Driftwood Absolute Return Fund Ltd.

**Why it qualifies.** This was a Funds & Asset Management engagement for the GP and Fund arising from a key-person event. The engagement letter identifies the fund's **Investor Advisory Committee** and expressly excludes representation of that committee—showing that it was an established LP-side governance body. The closing memorandum confirms that the IAC reviewed the proposed governance changes, met on July 29, 2024, and that the First Amendment became effective on August 26, 2024 after written consents from 38 of 47 limited partners.

I treated “Investor Advisory Committee” as an LP advisory committee for this query because the documents describe it as a committee of institutional limited partners with governance-review and consent-related functions.

**Key evidence relied on:**

- `documents/matters/1024-00002/Engagement/engagement-letter-darf-gp-advisory.docx` — identifies the Fund's Investor Advisory Committee and the LPA-governance advisory scope.
- `documents/matters/1024-00002/Transaction Documents/execution-first-amendment-ar-lpa.docx` — execution version of the First Amendment, effective August 26, 2024; recites the March 15, 2017 A&R LPA and the IAC's review.
- `documents/matters/1024-00002/Analyses & Memos/iac-presentation-memo.docx` — briefing materials for the five-member IAC.
- `documents/matters/1024-00002/Transaction Documents/form-of-lp-written-consent.docx` — LP consent mechanism for the LPA amendment.
- `documents/matters/1024-00002/Closing/engagement-closing-memo.docx` — confirms the effective amendment, IAC process, 38 consents, and completed matter.

### 3. Matter 1027-00002 — Ridgeline-Clarion Co-Invest, L.P.

**Why it qualifies.** This was an investor-side co-investment matter for Pellegrino Capital Group LLC. The engagement letter contemplated an LPAC seat, and the executed co-invest LPA goes further: §9.1 establishes a three-member **Limited Partner Advisory Committee**, with Pellegrino entitled to appoint one member while it holds an interest.

The execution version is dated January 30, 2026. The legal opinion was delivered in connection with the January 30 closing, and the funds-flow memorandum confirms that Pellegrino funded its $25 million commitment to the co-invest vehicle at that closing.

**Key evidence relied on:**

- `documents/matters/1027-00002/Engagement/engagement-letter-pellegrino.docx` — describes the co-investment and the proposed LPAC seat/right.
- `documents/matters/1027-00002/Transaction Documents/co-invest-lpa-execution-version.docx` — “Execution Version,” dated January 30, 2026; defines the LPAC and establishes it in §9.1.
- `documents/matters/1027-00002/Closing/enforceability-opinion-letter.docx` — confirms the January 30, 2026 closing and identifies the dated LPA as a reviewed transaction document.
- `documents/matters/1027-00002/Closing/funds-flow-memorandum.docx` — confirms the January 30, 2026 closing and Pellegrino's funded $25 million contribution.

## Exclusions and application of the signed-LPA filter

I did **not** count the following screened matters:

- **1002-00003 — Pinnacle Venture Fund II LP.** The engagement letter says the LPA was to be dated at the First Close, and the closing checklist is a First Close target checklist; the file does not establish an executed LPA. The LPAC/advisory-committee provisions were prospective side-letter terms.
- **1003-00002 — Harrowgate Private Equity Fund V LP.** The first-close checklist marks the LPA as a draft/redline under review, with the overall checklist “In Progress.” The LPAC charter and LPAC seats were still pending or subject to side-letter execution.
- **1004-00002 — Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I, LP.** The engagement materials describe a proposed fund, with the first LPA draft targeted for May 31, 2026 and the first close targeted for November 15, 2026; no signed LPA appears in the matter file.
- **1026-00001 — Meridian Peak Capital Partners Fund IV, L.P.** The matter reviewed an LPA dated December 20, 2023 and described an LPAC, but the closing memorandum expressly says the Fund's first close had not occurred, BFO's subscription agreement was never finalized or executed, and the negotiated side letter lapsed without execution. Because the file does not establish an executed Fund IV LPA, I applied the requested signed-LPA filter and excluded it.
- **1023-00001 — ICM Cascadia Co-Invest, LP.** The governance memorandum says the LP Agreement was only execution-ready and scheduled for later execution, and expressly states that no formal LPAC was established; the sole LP instead had direct consultation rights.

I also excluded tax-only or other non-Funds & Asset Management engagements that happened to involve fund entities or fund documents; the query asks for Funds & Asset Management matters, not every matter touching a fund."}

- `documents/matters/1001-00002/LP Consent & Notification/lpac-form-of-written-consent.docx` — records the LPAC written consent dated February 14, 2024.
- `documents/matters/1001-00002/Amended Governing Documents/lpa-amendment-no-1.docx` — Amendment No. 1 to the Fund LPA, effective February 28, 2024, following the LPAC consent.
- `documents/matters/1001-00002/Engagement & Administration/matter-closing-memo.docx` — confirms completion and execution of the restructuring documents and closure of the matter.
### 2. Matter 1024-00002 — Driftwood Absolute Return Fund Ltd.

**Why it qualifies.** This was a Funds & Asset Management engagement for the GP and Fund arising from a key-person event. The engagement letter identifies the fund's **Investor Advisory Committee** and expressly excludes representation of that committee—showing that it was an established LP-side governance body. The closing memorandum confirms that the IAC reviewed the proposed governance changes, met on July 29, 2024, and that the First Amendment became effective on August 26, 2024 after written consents from 38 of 47 limited partners.

I treated “Investor Advisory Committee” as an LP advisory committee for this query because the documents describe it as a committee of institutional limited partners with governance-review and consent-related functions.
**Key evidence relied on:**
- `documents/matters/1024-00002/Engagement/engagement-letter-darf-gp-advisory.docx` — identifies the Fund's Investor Advisory Committee and the LPA-governance advisory scope.

- `documents/matters/1024-00002/Transaction Documents/execution-first-amendment-ar-lpa.docx` — execution version of the First Amendment, effective August 26, 2024; recites the March 15, 2017 A&R LPA and the IAC's review.
- `documents/matters/1024-00002/Analyses & Memos/iac-presentation-memo.docx` — briefing materials for the five-member IAC.
- `documents/matters/1024-00002/Transaction Documents/form-of-lp-written-consent.docx` — LP consent mechanism for the LPA amendment.
- `documents/matters/1024-00002/Closing/engagement-closing-memo.docx` — confirms the effective amendment, IAC process, 38 consents, and completed matter.
### 3. Matter 1027-00002 — Ridgeline-Clarion Co-Invest, L.P.

**Why it qualifies.** This was an investor-side co-investment matter for Pellegrino Capital Group LLC. The engagement letter contemplated an LPAC seat, and the executed co-invest LPA goes further: §9.1 establishes a three-member **Limited Partner Advisory Committee**, with Pellegrino entitled to appoint one member while it holds an interest.

The execution version is dated January 30, 2026. The legal opinion was delivered in connection with the January 30 closing, and the funds-flow memorandum confirms that Pellegrino funded its $25 million commitment to the co-invest vehicle at that closing.
**Key evidence relied on:**
- `documents/matters/1027-00002/Engagement/engagement-letter-pellegrino.docx` — describes the co-investment and the proposed LPAC seat/right.
- `documents/matters/1027-00002/Transaction Documents/co-invest-lpa-execution-version.docx` — “Execution Version,” dated January 30, 2026; defines the LPAC and establishes it in §9.1.
- `documents/matters/1027-00002/Closing/enforceability-opinion-letter.docx` — confirms the January 30, 2026 closing and identifies the dated LPA as a reviewed transaction document.
- `documents/matters/1027-00002/Closing/funds-flow-memorandum.docx` — confirms the January 30, 2026 closing and Pellegrino's funded $25 million contribution.
## Exclusions and application of the signed-LPA filter
I did **not** count the following screened matters:

- **1002-00003 — Pinnacle Venture Fund II LP.** The engagement letter says the LPA was to be dated at the First Close, and the closing checklist is a First Close target checklist; the file does not establish an executed LPA. The LPAC/advisory-committee provisions were prospective side-letter terms.

- **1003-00002 — Harrowgate Private Equity Fund V LP.** The first-close checklist marks the LPA as a draft/redline under review, with the overall checklist “In Progress.” The LPAC charter and LPAC seats were still pending or subject to side-letter execution.

- **1004-00002 — Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I, LP.** The engagement materials describe a proposed fund, with the first LPA draft targeted for May 31, 2026 and the first close targeted for November 15, 2026; no signed LPA appears in the matter file.

- **1026-00001 — Meridian Peak Capital Partners Fund IV, L.P.** The matter reviewed an LPA dated December 20, 2023 and described an LPAC, but the closing memorandum expressly says the Fund's first close had not occurred, BFO's subscription agreement was never finalized or executed, and the negotiated side letter lapsed without execution. Because the file does not establish an executed Fund IV LPA, I applied the requested signed-LPA filter and excluded it.

- **1023-00001 — ICM Cascadia Co-Invest, LP.** The governance memorandum says the LP Agreement was only execution-ready and scheduled for later execution, and expressly states that no formal LPAC was established; the sole LP instead had direct consultation rights.

I also excluded tax-only or other non-Funds & Asset Management engagements that happened to involve fund entities or fund documents; the query asks for Funds & Asset Management matters, not every matter touching a fund.
